WASImageCropFaceYuNet.name: WASImageCropFaceYuNet
WASImageCropFaceYuNet.description: Find a face with YuNet and crop a square around it, together with the crop window Image Paste Face needs to put it back. The detector ships with the pack and runs in torch on whatever device ComfyUI is using, so there is nothing to install. Set features.yunet to false to leave this node out.

image.tooltip: The image to crop. A batch is cropped frame by frame to the same rectangle and comes back the same length.

top.tooltip: Distance in pixels from the top of the image to the top of the crop.

left.tooltip: Distance in pixels from the left of the image to the left of the crop.

right.tooltip: Position of the crop's right edge, in pixels from the left of the image. left 0 with right 256 gives a crop 256 pixels wide. A value past the image edge is trimmed to it.

bottom.tooltip: Position of the crop's bottom edge, in pixels from the top of the image. A value past the image edge is trimmed to it.

divisible_by.tooltip: Rounds the crop down to a multiple of this on both axes, which resamples it. 8 suits most latent models; 1 takes the exact rectangle away untouched.

output_tooltips: The cropped region, its width and height rounded down to a multiple of divisible_by, with a side shorter than that taken up to one whole step instead. At a divisible_by of 1 it is the exact rectangle asked for, carried through without resampling.
The crop window, for Image Paste Crop to put the result back in the right place at the right size.
Image Crop Location.name: Image Crop Location
Image Crop Location.description: Crop a rectangle given by its four edges, and pass on the crop window so the result can be pasted back later. Rounding the crop with divisible_by saves a sampler rounding the size itself: 8 suits most latent models, and 16, 32 or 64 the ones that ask for a coarser step. 1 rounds nothing. A side shorter than divisible_by is taken up to one whole step rather than down to nothing.

image.tooltip: The image to crop. A batch is cropped frame by frame to the same square and comes back the same length.

x.tooltip: Horizontal centre of the square, in pixels from the left of the image.

y.tooltip: Vertical centre of the square, in pixels from the top of the image. With x, 0/0 asks for a square centred on the top-left corner, which slides down and right until it fits.

size.tooltip: Length of each side of the square, in pixels. A size larger than the image gives the whole image instead.

divisible_by.tooltip: Rounds the crop down to a multiple of this on both axes, which resamples it. 8 suits most latent models; 1 takes the exact square away untouched.

output_tooltips: The cropped square, its width and height rounded down to a multiple of divisible_by, with a side shorter than that taken up to one whole step instead. At a divisible_by of 1 it is the exact region asked for, carried through without resampling.
The crop window, for Image Paste Crop to put the result back in the right place at the right size.
Image Crop Square Location.name: Image Crop Square Location
Image Crop Square Location.description: Crop a square region centred on a point, and pass on the crop window so the result can be pasted back later. Rounding the crop with divisible_by saves a sampler rounding the size itself: 8 suits most latent models, and 16, 32 or 64 the ones that ask for a coarser step. 1 rounds nothing. A side shorter than divisible_by is taken up to one whole step rather than down to nothing.

image.tooltip: The images to draw on. Every image in the batch gets the same text, so a caption applies across a whole sequence in one node.

text.tooltip: The text to draw. Line breaks are kept. Tokens such as `[time]` and `[hostname]` resolve before drawing, which is how a frame carries the date it was rendered.

font_size.tooltip: Height of the text in points. A caption on a 1024-pixel image reads at around 24 to 40; a title wants considerably more.

text_color.tooltip: Colour of the glyphs, as #RRGGBB, #RRGGBBAA or a name such as 'white'. The eight-digit form carries its own transparency, which is how a watermark is made faint without fading the outline with it.

position.tooltip: Where the block of text sits on the image. The corners and edges hold back by the margin below; 'middle center' ignores it.

align.tooltip: How the lines line up with each other inside the block. Separate from position, which places the block: a block anchored bottom right can still be left-aligned inside itself.

offset_x.tooltip: Pixels to move the text right of where position put it. Negative moves it left. For nudging a block off an anchor rather than placing it from scratch.

offset_y.tooltip: Pixels to move the text down. Negative moves it up.

margin.tooltip: Space held back from every edge, so an edge-anchored caption does not touch the border. Ignored on whichever axis the position centres on.

line_spacing.tooltip: Multiplier on the font's own line height. 1.0 is single spaced; 1.2 to 1.5 is easier to read for a paragraph of several lines.

wrap_width.tooltip: Width in pixels to wrap the text at. 0 turns wrapping off and only the line breaks already in the text are honoured. A word wider than this on its own is left whole and overhangs rather than being split.

stroke_width.tooltip: Width of an outline drawn around every glyph. 1 or 2 is what keeps a caption legible over a picture whose brightness changes underneath it. 0 draws no outline.

stroke_color.tooltip: Colour of the outline. Read only when stroke_width is 1 or more.

background_color.tooltip: Colour of a panel drawn behind the text. Empty draws no panel. A half-transparent #000000B4 is the usual subtitle treatment, and is more readable than an outline over a busy picture.

background_padding.tooltip: How far the panel extends past the text on every side. Read only when background_color is set.

opacity.tooltip: How much of the finished text shows, 0.0 to 1.0. Applied to the text, its outline and its panel together, so a faint watermark stays consistent instead of the outline surviving the fade.

font.tooltip: Which typeface to draw with. The DejaVu faces cover the most ground; `Mono` gives every character the same width, which stops a frame counter jittering.

output_tooltips: The images with the text drawn on them.
The text as a mask, white where a glyph, outline or panel was drawn. Feeds an inpaint region or a blend factor without drawing the text twice.
WASImageDrawText.name: WASImageDrawText
WASImageDrawText.description: Draw text over an image, with wrapping, alignment, an outline and a background panel. Returns the picture and the text as a mask. The font list is built from disk: drop .ttf, .otf or .ttc files into the fonts folder beside config.yaml, at ComfyUI/user/was-node-suite/fonts, and they appear in the menu named after the file. Put them there rather than inside the pack, which an update overwrites. The DejaVu faces cover the most ground and are the safe choice for text not known in advance; the Liberation faces match Arial, Times New Roman and Courier New width for width, so a caption composed against one of those breaks its lines in the same places. A font that cannot be opened falls back to the picked one, then to a small built-in bitmap face that ignores font_size.

consistent.tooltip: The picture to keep. Its low frequencies and all of its colour are carried through, so this is the one that decides structure and tone.

sharp.tooltip: The picture to take detail from. Only its luma high frequencies are used, and only where it has more of them than the first picture. Must be the same size and hold the same number of frames.

cutoff.tooltip: Where low stops and high starts, as a fraction of the picture's own frequency range rather than in pixels. Lower keeps more of the first picture; higher hands more of the image over to the second.

order.tooltip: How abruptly the split happens. 1 is a gentle roll-off, high values approach a hard cut and can ring around strong edges.

strength.tooltip: How much of the blended detail to add back. 0 returns the first picture blurred to the cutoff, 1 is the intended amount, and above 1 exaggerates.

border.tooltip: Pixels around the edge left as the first picture. A transform of a whole frame rings slightly at its boundary, and this hides it. 0 blends right to the edge.

output_tooltips: The first picture's structure carrying the second one's detail.
WASImageFrequencyBlend.name: WASImageFrequencyBlend
WASImageFrequencyBlend.description: Split two pictures into low and high frequencies and keep the low ones from the first while taking the high ones from whichever has more detail there. For a steady pass and a sharper pass of the same shot, this keeps the steadiness and gains the detail. Colour comes from the first picture only.

images.tooltip: The frames the matte is solved against. Each one is run on its own and comes back at the size it went in at.

masks.tooltip: The rough mask, white where the subject is. A hard cut-out from Image Remove Background, CLIPSeg Masking or SAM is what this is for. One mask is used for every frame; a batch is paired frame by frame.

certain_foreground.tooltip: Mask level above which a pixel is certainly the subject, on a 0 to 255 scale. 240 trusts only what the mask calls solid; 128 trusts more of it and leaves a narrower band to solve.

certain_background.tooltip: Mask level below which a pixel is certainly not the subject, on a 0 to 255 scale. 10 trusts only what the mask calls empty; 64 trusts more of it.

band.tooltip: Pixels pulled back off both certain regions, which is what the matte is solved across. 0 = solve nothing and answer the mask; 10 = a 10px band, enough for a soft edge; 40 = enough for flyaway hair.

unmix_foreground.tooltip: `on` also estimates the subject's own colour with the background taken out of it, which removes a fringe. `off` answers the frame unchanged on that output and is several times faster.

output_tooltips: The solved matte, white where the subject is, soft across the band.

The subject's colour with the background unmixed out of it. Composite this rather than the original frame, or the old background follows the edge onto the new one. A frame carrying light above white comes back on the scale it arrived on.
The foreground with the matte as its fourth channel, ready for Add Layer, Join Image with Alpha or a PNG save.
WASImageMatte.name: WASImageMatte
WASImageMatte.description: Turn a rough mask into a matte that holds hair, fur, smoke and motion blur. The band between the certain foreground and the certain background is solved against the picture's own colours, so a hard cut-out from a segmenter or a threshold comes back with a soft, correct edge. The foreground output is the subject's colour with the background unmixed out of it, which is what stops a green or a white fringe following a cut-out onto a new plate.

red_channel.tooltip: Image whose brightness becomes the red channel. All three inputs must be the same size.

green_channel.tooltip: Image whose brightness becomes the green channel.

blue_channel.tooltip: Image whose brightness becomes the blue channel.

output_tooltips: The recombined colour image. Feeding the same picture to all three inputs gives a grey copy of it.
Image Mix RGB Channels.name: Image Mix RGB Channels
Image Mix RGB Channels.description: Combine three greyscale images into one colour image, using their brightness as the red, green and blue channels.

image.tooltip: The full-size image to paste into, normally the same one the crop was taken from.

crop_image.tooltip: The processed crop to paste back. It is resized to the size recorded in crop_data, so it may be scaled up or down on the way in.

crop_data.tooltip: The crop window from Image Crop Location or Image Crop Square Location, which says where the crop belongs. Image Crop Face passes False here when it found no face, and that returns the image untouched with a black mask.

crop_blending.tooltip: How much of each pasted edge is faded out, as a fraction of the crop. 0.0 gives a hard visible seam, 0.25 fades the outer quarter of each edge, and 1.0 fades right across the crop so only its centre is fully opaque.

crop_sharpening.tooltip: How many sharpening passes to run on the crop before pasting, to recover detail lost to resizing. 0 pastes it as it is; 3 is the strongest and tends to leave halos.

output_tooltips: The full-size image with the crop composited back into it.
The blend mask the paste used, full size and black outside the window. White is where the crop fully replaced the image, so it shows how far the seam was faded.
Image Paste Crop.name: Image Paste Crop
Image Paste Crop.description: Paste a cropped image back into the picture it was taken from, at the window a crop node recorded, with a soft seam around it.

image.tooltip: The image to paste into, which sets the canvas size.

crop_image.tooltip: The image to paste in. It is stretched to the rectangle, so its own aspect ratio is not preserved.

top.tooltip: Distance in pixels from the top of the image to the top of the paste.

left.tooltip: Distance in pixels from the left of the image to the left of the paste.

right.tooltip: Position of the paste's right edge, in pixels from the left of the image. left 0 with right 256 pastes into a 256-pixel-wide area. Values past the image edge are trimmed to it.

bottom.tooltip: Position of the paste's bottom edge, in pixels from the top of the image. Values past the image edge are trimmed to it.

crop_blending.tooltip: How soft the edge of the paste is. 0.0 gives a hard rectangle, and 0.25 blurs the edge over roughly an eighth of the rectangle's longer side.

crop_sharpening.tooltip: How many sharpening passes to run on the pasted image after it is stretched, to recover detail lost to the resize. 0 pastes it as it is; 3 is the strongest and tends to leave halos.

output_tooltips: The image with the second one composited into the rectangle.

The blend mask the paste used, white where the pasted image fully covers and fading to black across the softened edge. A rectangle too thin to hold the whole fade never reaches white, which is the sign to lower crop_blending.
Image Paste Crop by Location.name: Image Paste Crop by Location
Image Paste Crop by Location.description: Paste one image into a rectangle of another, stretching it to fit and softening the edge. A crop_blending of 1.0 blurs so far that little of the pasted image stays fully opaque. The fade is always measured from the rectangle's longer side, so on a long thin rectangle a high value leaves the whole paste faint rather than sharply cut. Lower it until the paste reads at the strength wanted.

image.tooltip: The full-size image to paste into, normally the same one the face was cropped from.

crop_image.tooltip: The reworked face to paste back. It is resized to the size recorded in crop_data, so it may be scaled up or down on the way in.

crop_data.tooltip: The crop window from Image Crop Face, which says where the face belongs. That node passes False here when it found no face, and this returns the image untouched with a black mask.

crop_blending.tooltip: How much of each pasted edge is faded out, as a fraction of the crop. 0.0 gives a hard visible seam, 0.25 fades the outer quarter of each edge, and 1.0 fades right across the crop so only its centre is fully opaque.

crop_sharpening.tooltip: How many sharpening passes to run on the face before pasting, to recover detail lost to resizing. 0 pastes it as it is; 3 is the strongest and tends to leave halos around the eyes and hair.

output_tooltips: The full-size image with the face composited back into it.
The blend mask the paste used, full size and black outside the window. White is where the face fully replaced the image, so it shows how far the seam was faded.
Image Paste Face.name: Image Paste Face
Image Paste Face.description: Paste a face crop back into the picture Image Crop Face took it from, with a soft seam around it.

images.tooltip: The images to pixelate. Each one is handled on its own.

pixelation_size.tooltip: Width in pixels the image is reduced to before being blown back up, which sets how big the blocks look. 16 gives very coarse blocks, 164 a recognisable picture, and 480 a subtle effect. An image already smaller than this is not touched.

num_colors.tooltip: How many colours to keep. 2 gives two-tone, 16 is a classic 8-bit look, and 256 keeps most of the original shading.

init_mode.tooltip: How the colour reduction starts. `k-means++` spreads the starting colours apart and usually finds the better palette; `random` is quicker and can miss a colour that covers little of the image; `none` skips the colour reduction altogether and only shrinks the image.

max_iterations.tooltip: Refinement passes the colour reduction is allowed. 100 settles almost any picture; 10 stops early and is quicker but coarser; 256 is the most it will spend. Read only when init_mode is not `none`.

dither.tooltip: `on` scatters the rounding error into neighbouring pixels, which trades flat bands of colour for a fine speckle and makes a small palette look richer; `off` leaves the flat areas flat.

dither_mode.tooltip: Which dither to use when dither is on. `FloydSteinberg` gives a fine organic stipple; `Ordered` snaps to a power-of-two number of levels first, giving a coarser, more regular texture.

color_palettes.tooltip: One palette of '#rrggbb' lines per image, as Image Color Palette emits. Connect it to repaint the result in those colours instead of the ones found in the image. Leave it unconnected to keep the image's own colours.

color_palette_mode.tooltip: How a pixel is matched to a palette colour. `Perceptual` picks the closest colour as the eye sees it, and is the one to reach for.

reverse_palette.tooltip: On flips the palette end to end before matching, which inverts a dark-to-light ramp. `Linear` and `Luminance Ramp` change visibly; the modes that match on colour rather than on position do not.

palette_dither.tooltip: How the error left by palette matching is spread, in `Perceptual` mode. `FloydSteinberg` gives an organic stipple; `Bayer` a fixed 8x8 pattern that stays still.

palette_smooth.tooltip: Whether `Luminance Ramp` blends between neighbouring palette colours. On, the palette reads as a continuous gradient and shading survives the mapping. Off, every pixel snaps to one palette colour, banding the picture into exactly that many tones, which is usually what pixel art wants.

palette_blend.tooltip: How much of the palette result replaces the colours under it, in the two perceptual modes. 1.0 is the palette alone; lower values let the reduced original show through, which softens a colourised plate back towards its own hues.

palette_normalize.tooltip: Whether `Luminance Ramp` stretches the palette across each image's darkest and lightest values. Off by default, which reads brightness absolutely and keeps a sequence steady.

output_tooltips: The pixelated images, back at their original size.
Image Pixelate.name: Image Pixelate
Image Pixelate.description: Turn an image into pixel art with large blocky pixels and a small number of colours, optionally dithered or remapped onto a supplied palette. color_palette_mode is ignored with no palette connected, and `Perceptual` is the only mode palette_dither works with. `Luminance Ramp` throws the original colour away and places each pixel along the palette by brightness; set init_mode to `none` with it, since reducing the colours first destroys the shading it reads. The four older modes compare raw channel numbers: `Brightness` takes the closest colour overall, `Tonal` matches brightness only so hues swap freely, `BrightnessAndTonal` weighs both, and `Linear` indexes the palette by the red value for a hard banded remap. palette_dither diffuses against the palette itself, unlike dither, which runs first and is then re-quantised; `Bayer` is the one for a sequence.

images.tooltip: The images to cut out. Each is handled on its own.

mode.tooltip: Which part of the image to clear, decided on brightness alone. `background` clears every pixel at or below the threshold, so a dark backdrop goes and the light part is kept. `foreground` clears every pixel at or above it, so a white studio sweep goes instead.

threshold.tooltip: Brightness the cut is made at, 0 for black and 255 for white; 127 cuts at mid grey. In `background` mode everything this dark or darker is cleared, so raising it clears more of the image; in `foreground` mode everything this bright or brighter is cleared, so raising it clears less.

threshold_tolerance.tooltip: How much the brightness is blurred before the cut, in pixels. Small values follow the edge closely but keep speckles; larger values give a smoother outline that creeps in over fine detail such as hair.

output_tooltips: The images with an alpha channel, transparent wherever the threshold cut them away.
Image Remove Background (Alpha).name: Image Remove Background (Alpha)
Image Remove Background (Alpha).description: Make the brightest or darkest part of an image transparent, judged on brightness alone. Best on a flat backdrop, such as a white studio sweep.

image.tooltip: The image to repaint.

target_red.tooltip: Red level of the colour being looked for, 0 to 255.

target_green.tooltip: Green level of the colour being looked for, 0 to 255.

target_blue.tooltip: Blue level of the colour being looked for, 0 to 255. The three together default to white.

replace_red.tooltip: Red level of the colour painted over every match, 0 to 255.

replace_green.tooltip: Green level of the colour painted over every match, 0 to 255.

replace_blue.tooltip: Blue level of the colour painted over every match, 0 to 255. Leave all three at 255 and the matched area is painted white; set them to 0 for black.

clip_threshold.tooltip: How far a pixel may differ from the target colour and still be repainted. 0 repaints only exact matches, 10 tolerates slight gradients and compression noise, and a high value repaints most of the image.

output_tooltips: The image with every matched pixel repainted in the replacement colour.
Image Remove Color.name: Image Remove Color
Image Remove Color.description: Find every pixel close to one colour and repaint it in another, turning a white background black, for instance.

images.tooltip: The images to make tileable. Each one is processed separately.

blending.tooltip: How much of each side the cross-fade between edges spans, as a fraction. 0.0 answers the image unchanged; 0.4 fades the outer 40 percent, which suits most textures; 0.5 is the most the edges leave room for. The answer is smaller by this fraction on each side.

tiled.tooltip: `on` = the tile repeated into a grid, which is how the join is checked; `off` = the single tile, which is what to feed onward.

tiles.tooltip: How many copies along each side of the grid when tiled is on. 2 gives a 2x2 preview of four copies; 4 gives sixteen. Ignored when tiled is off.

output_tooltips: The tileable images, or the grids of them, one per image in. A grid is tiles times larger on each side than the tile.
Image Seamless Texture.name: Image Seamless Texture
Image Seamless Texture.description: Turn an image into a seamlessly tiling texture by blending its opposite edges into each other, and optionally show it repeated as a grid. The tile is smaller than the source by the blended fraction on each side.

image.tooltip: The image to read the channel from.

channel.tooltip: Which channel to keep. Skin and warm light are brightest in `red`, foliage and most detail in `green`, sky and shadows in `blue`. The other two channels are discarded.

output_tooltips: The chosen channel as a grey image the same size as the input, suitable for use as a mask or a depth-like map.
Image Select Channel.name: Image Select Channel
Image Select Channel.description: Extract one colour channel and return it as a greyscale image, where white means that channel was at full strength.

image.tooltip: The image to search for the colour in.

red.tooltip: Red level of the colour to look for, 0 to 255.

green.tooltip: Green level of the colour to look for, 0 to 255.

blue.tooltip: Blue level of the colour to look for, 0 to 255. Together the three make one colour: 255/255/255 is white, 0/255/0 is pure green.

variance.tooltip: How far each channel may differ from the target and still count as a match. 0 keeps only the exact colour, 10 tolerates slight shading, and 255 matches every pixel in the image.

output_tooltips: The matching pixels at their original colour, with every other pixel black.
Image Select Color.name: Image Select Color
Image Select Color.description: Keep only the pixels close to one colour and turn the rest black, for isolating a green screen, a sky or a single painted object.

image.tooltip: The image to reduce. Colour is discarded; only brightness is read.

threshold.tooltip: Brightness a pixel must reach to come out white, where 0.0 is black and 1.0 is white. 0.5 splits the image at mid grey; lower it to keep more of the image white, raise it to keep only the brightest highlights.

output_tooltips: The two-tone result, one image per image in. Every pixel is either fully black or fully white.
Image Threshold.name: Image Threshold
Image Threshold.description: Turn an image into flat black and white: anything brighter than the threshold becomes white and everything else becomes black.

image.tooltip: The image to cut up. Only the first image of a batch is used.

num_tiles.tooltip: How many tiles to aim for. Square numbers divide evenly, 4 gives a 2x2 grid and 16 a 4x4 one, while other counts leave a part-row or part-column and so return a few tiles more than requested.

output_tooltips: The tiles as one batch, ordered left to right then top to bottom. Every tile is the same size; edge tiles are padded with black where the image ran out.
Image Tiled.name: Image Tiled
Image Tiled.description: Cut an image into a grid of smaller tiles and hand them on as a batch, for processing a large picture a piece at a time.

layers.tooltip: The stack to read. Wire in Add Layer, Layers From Bounding Boxes or anything else answering a LAYERS document.

placement.tooltip: `on the canvas` pads every layer out to the document's canvas at the position it sits, so the frames line up and can be recombined; `at its own size` crops each to its own pixels, which suits sending one layer through a filter.

hidden_layers.tooltip: Whether a layer the compositor has switched off is read too. `off` skips it, which matches what Create Layered Image draws; `on` reads the whole document.

output_tooltips: One frame per picture, lowest in the stack first, drawn at the size, angle and flip the layer carries. A layer holding a batch answers one frame per picture.
What each layer covers, white where it paints. A layer with no mask of its own covers its whole rectangle.
Where each layer sits on the canvas, one row per layer, for Bounded Image Crop, Bounds to Mask or Draw Image Bounds.
What the compositor calls each layer, in the same order.
How many frames came out, for a switch that handles none.
WASLayersToImageBatch.name: WASLayersToImageBatch
WASLayersToImageBatch.description: Take a layer stack apart: one frame per layer, its coverage as a mask, where it sits as bounds, and its name. Create Layered Image flattens a stack into a single picture, so this is the way back out of one, and it puts every layer of a compositor document, a detector's regions or a pasted-together plate through the rest of the pack one frame at a time.

images.tooltip: The images to bend. A batch is warped one image at a time and comes back the same length, and every image keeps the width and height it went in at.

displacement_maps.tooltip: The map that says how far to push each pixel, read as brightness: black does not move, white moves by the full amplitude. Any size is accepted.

amplitude.tooltip: How far a fully white area of the map moves a pixel, in pixels, on both axes at once. 25 gives a gentle ripple, 200 a heavy smear, 0 leaves the image alone, and a negative value pushes up and left. Values past the image's own width or height read outside it and raise an error.

output_tooltips: The warped images, in the order they arrived, as RGB.
Image Displacement Warp.name: Image Displacement Warp
Image Displacement Warp.description: Bend an image by a second, greyscale image. Bright areas of the map pull pixels diagonally down and right, dark areas leave them where they are, which turns any texture into a ripple, smear or melt. Each pixel is read one at a time, so a large image takes a while. A displacement map is scaled to cover the image and centre-cropped, and where the map batch is shorter than the image batch the last map is reused for the rest. Smooth maps such as clouds or a blurred gradient give flowing results, and sharp ones tear the image.

images.tooltip: The images to mirror.

mode.tooltip: Which axis to mirror across. `horizontal` swaps left and right, as a mirror does; `vertical` swaps top and bottom, as still water does.

output_tooltips: The mirrored images, in the order they arrived.
Image Flip.name: Image Flip
Image Flip.description: Mirror every image in the batch. The size does not change and no pixels are resampled, so nothing is lost.

images.tooltip: The frames to bend. Each one gets the same distortion and comes back at the size it went in at.

k1.tooltip: The main radial term. 0.0 = straight, -0.15 = a gentle barrel, -0.5 = a strong fisheye bow, 0.15 = a pincushion that takes a barrel back out.

k2.tooltip: A second radial term acting furthest from the centre. 0.0 = none, 0.05 = pulls the very corners back after a strong k1, which is how a real lens profile is written.

scale.tooltip: Zoom applied with the bend. 1.0 = none, so a barrel leaves empty corners; 1.2 = zoomed in far enough to fill them; 0.8 = pulled back to keep everything the frame held.

dispersion.tooltip: How far red and blue are scaled apart, growing towards the corners. 0.0 = none, 0.004 = a faint colour fringe at the edges, 0.02 = an obvious one.

edge.tooltip: What fills the space the bend opens up. `hold the edge` smears the outermost pixel out; `mirror` folds the frame back on itself; `empty` leaves it black.

output_tooltips: The frames with the distortion applied.
WASImageLensDistortion.name: WASImageLensDistortion
WASImageLensDistortion.description: Bow the frame outwards or pinch it inwards, and split the colour channels apart across the radius. Negative k1 barrels, which is what a wide lens or an action camera does; positive k1 pincushions, which takes that bow out of footage that already has it. Image Chromatic Aberration splits the channels without moving the geometry; this does both at once, as a real lens does.

image.tooltip: The image to place on the larger canvas.

feathering.tooltip: How far the image's own edges fade out, in pixels. 0 leaves a hard edge, and the fade reaches roughly three times this far in.

feather_second_pass.tooltip: `on` runs a second, narrower fade that restores the middle of the image to full opacity and keeps the softening near the edge. `off` applies the wide fade alone, which leaves the whole image noticeably lighter.

left_padding.tooltip: Empty space added on the left, in pixels.

right_padding.tooltip: Empty space added on the right, in pixels.

top_padding.tooltip: Empty space added above, in pixels.

bottom_padding.tooltip: Empty space added below, in pixels. The four margins are independent, so 8 on three sides and 512 on one extends the image in a single direction.

target_width.tooltip: Pad out to this width instead of using the four side amounts, which is what outpainting wants. 0 leaves the sides in charge. The picture is centred and a target narrower than the picture pads nothing.

target_height.tooltip: Pad out to this height instead of using the four side amounts. 0 leaves the sides in charge.

output_tooltips: The padded canvas, with the faded image on it and transparency everywhere else.
The area to fill, as an image: white where the canvas is empty, black where the image is solid, grey across the fade. Convert it with Image to Mask to wire it into an inpainting node.
Image Padding.name: Image Padding
Image Padding.description: Put an image on a larger empty canvas and fade its edges out, then return the canvas and a mask of everything that was added. Feed both to an inpainting pass to fill the new space. A larger feathering gives that fill more of a run-up and eats further into the original: 120 fades most of a 512 pixel image and wipes out anything smaller than about 480 pixels altogether, so keep it under a quarter of the image's shorter side.

images.tooltip: The frames to warp. Each one gets the same mapping and comes back at the output size.

top_left_x.tooltip: Where the frame's top left corner lands, across the output, in pixels. 0 = the output's own top left, 120 = 120px in from it.

top_left_y.tooltip: Where the frame's top left corner lands, down the output, in pixels. 0 = flush with the top, 80 = 80px down.

top_right_x.tooltip: Where the frame's top right corner lands, measured in from the right edge. 0 = flush with it, 120 = 120px in.

top_right_y.tooltip: Where the frame's top right corner lands, down the output, in pixels. 0 = flush with the top, 80 = 80px down.

bottom_right_x.tooltip: Where the frame's bottom right corner lands, measured in from the right edge. 0 = flush with it, 120 = 120px in.

bottom_right_y.tooltip: Where the frame's bottom right corner lands, measured up from the bottom edge. 0 = flush with it, 80 = 80px up.

bottom_left_x.tooltip: Where the frame's bottom left corner lands, across the output, in pixels. 0 = flush with the left, 120 = 120px in.

bottom_left_y.tooltip: Where the frame's bottom left corner lands, measured up from the bottom edge. 0 = flush with it, 80 = 80px up.

width.tooltip: Width of the answer in pixels. 0 = the same width the frames came in at; 1920 makes room for corners pushed outside them.

height.tooltip: Height of the answer in pixels. 0 = the same height the frames came in at; 1080 makes room for corners pushed outside them.

edge.tooltip: What fills the space outside the warped picture. `empty` leaves it black, which is what a composite wants; `hold the edge` smears the outermost pixel out; `mirror` folds the frame back.

output_tooltips: The warped frames, at the output size.
White where the warped picture landed, black around it, for compositing it onto a plate.
WASImagePerspective.name: WASImagePerspective
WASImagePerspective.description: Drag each corner of the frame somewhere else and let the picture follow. That maps a flat render onto a surface seen at an angle: a poster onto a wall, a screen into a photograph, a label onto a box. It also takes a keystone back out of a plate shot off-axis. Image Displacement Warp bends the picture locally; this is the one straight-line mapping a camera makes.

image.tooltip: The images to scale.

mode.tooltip: `rescale` multiplies the current size by rescale_factor and ignores the two size fields. `resize` goes to resize_width by resize_height and ignores the factor.

supersample.tooltip: `true` resamples through eight times the target size and back down, which smooths jagged edges when enlarging; `false` resizes in one step. Both take the same memory. Ignored under `crop or pad`, which resamples nothing.

resampling.tooltip: How pixels are interpolated in `rescale` mode. `lanczos` is the sharpest and the slowest, `bicubic` and `bilinear` are progressively softer and quicker, `nearest` copies the closest pixel and keeps hard edges and pixel art crisp. `resize` mode follows resampling above.

rescale_factor.tooltip: Size multiplier used in rescale mode. 2.0 doubles both sides, 0.5 halves them, 1.0 leaves the size alone.

resize_width.tooltip: Target width in pixels for resize mode, rounded up to the next multiple of 8: 1000 gives 1000, 1001 gives 1008.

resize_height.tooltip: Target height in pixels for resize mode, rounded up to the next multiple of 8. Set it independently of the width; resize_mode decides what becomes of the aspect ratio.

resize_mode.tooltip: How the picture meets the requested size in `resize` mode. `stretch` takes both sides exactly and distorts, which is what this node has always done. `fit and pad`: the whole picture inside pad_color bars. `fill and crop`: fills the size, the overhang is cut. `crop or pad`: no resampling at all. Ignored in `rescale`.

align.tooltip: Which part of the picture survives a crop, and which side takes the wider pad bar. `top center` suits portraits, where a centred crop takes the forehead off. Ignored in `stretch` and in `rescale` mode.

pad_color.tooltip: Fill for space the picture does not cover; STRING. Any Pillow colour: `#RRGGBB`, a name, or `#RRGGBBAA`. Empty is transparent, which only shows on a batch carrying alpha. Seen in `fit and pad` and `crop or pad`. Eg: white

multiple_of.tooltip: Round both sides of a `resize` down to a multiple of this, which is how a size is made safe for a latent. 8 suits most models, 16 and 64 some others. 0 leaves the size alone. Ignored in `rescale`.

output_tooltips: The scaled images, all at the new size.
Width of the delivered images in pixels: the rescaled width in `rescale` mode, or the requested width after the multiple of 8 and after multiple_of in `resize` mode.
Height of the delivered images in pixels: the rescaled height in `rescale` mode, or the requested height after the multiple of 8 and after multiple_of in `resize` mode.
Image Resize.name: Image Resize
Image Resize.description: Scale every image in the batch, either by a multiplier or to an exact width and height. Rescale mode holds the source proportions. Resize mode goes to the two sides given, each rounded up to the next multiple of 8, so a requested 1001 is delivered as 1008, and resize_mode decides how the picture meets them: padded, cropped, stretched, or left unresampled. Neither mode goes below one pixel on a side. The whole batch is resampled on the GPU at full precision, so values above 1.0 survive.

images.tooltip: The images to turn. Every image in a batch gets the same rotation and comes back in the order it arrived, with its width and height swapped at 90 or 270 degrees in `transpose` mode.

mode.tooltip: `transpose` turns the image by moving whole pixels, so a portrait image becomes landscape and nothing is lost. `internal` rotates inside the original frame instead, which keeps the width and height as they were and crops the corners off a quarter turn of a non-square image.

rotation.tooltip: How far to turn, in degrees counter-clockwise. Only multiples of 90 are applied: 90, 180 and 270 turn, while 0 and 360 leave the image alone.

sampler.tooltip: Filter used when pixels have to be interpolated. Quarter turns land on whole pixels, so this changes nothing at any rotation the node accepts; `nearest` is the cheapest of the three.

output_tooltips: The rotated images, in the order they arrived.
Image Rotate.name: Image Rotate
Image Rotate.description: Turn every image in the batch counter-clockwise by a multiple of 90 degrees. Anything between multiples is rounded down, so 100 degrees rotates by 90.

image_a.tooltip: The image that stays in place, and the one whose other dimension sets the canvas size.

stitch.tooltip: Which side of image_a image_b goes on. `left` and `right` build a wide canvas, `top` and `bottom` a tall one.

feathering.tooltip: Width of the blended overlap in pixels. 0 butts the images together with a hard edge; 50 fades them over 50 pixels, which hides the seam between two views of the same scene. The seam is cut out of the pair, so a feather wider than a slot narrows the result, and stitching many slots that way narrows it further.

image_c.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_d.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_e.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_f.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_g.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_h.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_i.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_j.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_k.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_l.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_m.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_n.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_o.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_p.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_q.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_r.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_s.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_t.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_u.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_v.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_w.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_x.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_y.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

image_z.tooltip: A further image, stitched on after the one before it in the same direction. The interface reveals the next slot as this one is filled.

output_tooltips: One image holding both inputs, blended across the join.
Image Stitch.name: Image Stitch
Image Stitch.description: Put image_b against one edge of image_a on a single canvas, fading the two together across the join. The images overlap by the feathering width, so the canvas is that much shorter than the two laid end to end. The canvas takes its other side from image_a alone, which leaves black where a smaller image_b does not reach and crops a larger one.

image.tooltip: The background. The result is this image's size, whatever the overlay's.

image_overlay.tooltip: The image placed on top of the background.

width.tooltip: Width the overlay is scaled to, in pixels, ignoring its own aspect ratio. Must be above 0.

height.tooltip: Height the overlay is scaled to, in pixels, ignoring its own aspect ratio. Must be above 0.

X.tooltip: Horizontal position of the overlay's left edge, in pixels from the left of the background. 0 is flush left; negative values push it off the left edge.

Y.tooltip: Vertical position of the overlay's top edge, in pixels down from the top of the background. 0 is flush with the top; negative values push it off the top edge.

rotation.tooltip: How far to turn the overlay before scaling, in degrees counter-clockwise. Negative values turn it clockwise. The overlay is squeezed back into width by height afterwards, so a rotated overlay comes out narrower than an unrotated one.

feathering.tooltip: Width of the fade around the overlay's edge, in pixels. 0 gives a hard edge; 32 fades the outer 32 pixels to transparent, which blends the overlay into the background.

output_tooltips: The background with the overlay composited onto it, in RGBA. Nodes that need three channels want Images to RGB after this.
Image Transpose.name: Image Transpose
Image Transpose.description: Scale, rotate and paste image_overlay onto image, with an optional soft edge. The result is the size of image and carries an alpha channel.

audio.tooltip: The sound to measure, from Load Video (Advanced), Load Video (Upload) or any node with an AUDIO output. A file with no sound track answers nothing on that socket, which reads here as zeroes rather than an error.

silence_threshold.tooltip: How loud the loudest sample may be and still count as silence. 0.0 = only a track that is silent to the last bit; 0.001 is about -60 dBFS and also catches a noise floor or a tail of dither. Sample values run 0.0 to 1.0.

output_tooltips: Seconds one clip plays for, which is samples divided by sample_rate. 0.0 where there is no sound. Feed it to a frame count so a render comes out the length of the music.
Samples per second the clip was recorded at: 44100 for CD audio, 48000 for most video. 0 where nothing readable arrived. Compare two of them before mixing clips that would not line up.
How many channels one clip holds: 1 = mono, 2 = stereo. 0 where nothing readable arrived.
How many samples each channel of one clip holds. At 48000 Hz, 480000 samples is ten seconds.
How many clips are stacked in this AUDIO. A loader answers 1; more than that comes from a node that stacked several together.
True when the loudest sample sits at or below silence_threshold, and true for a missing or unreadable AUDIO. Wire it into a switch to skip an encode that would only write a silent track.

The loudest single sample anywhere in the batch, as a distance from zero: 0.0 = silence, 1.0 = full scale, above 1.0 = clipped when it is written out. Use it to catch a take that needs the level pulled down.

The average level across the whole batch, on the same 0.0 to 1.0 scale as peak. It tracks how loud something sounds far better than peak does: music mastered loud sits near 0.2, a quiet dialogue take nearer 0.02.

The whole reading as one line, `44100 Hz, 2 ch, 132300 samples, 3.000 s, batch 1, peak 0.813, rms 0.204`, with `, silent` on the end where it is. `no audio` where nothing readable arrived. The same text is drawn on the node.
WASAudioMetadata.name: WASAudioMetadata
WASAudioMetadata.description: Read what an AUDIO is carrying: how long it plays for, the rate it was sampled at, how many channels and samples each clip holds, how many clips are stacked in it, and how loud it is as a peak and an average level. The whole reading is drawn on the node and emitted as one line of text. A load that found no sound, or handed over something unreadable, answers zeroes and is_silent true rather than stopping the run, so a graph can branch on the silence before it reaches an encoder.

folder.tooltip: Which folder to read. A bare 'input', 'output' or 'temp' is that folder itself; 'plates/shot_01 [input]' is that folder below it. Any folder added under paths.allow_read in config.yaml is listed under its own name, and so are the folders inside it.

pattern.tooltip: Which entries to list, as a glob. `*` takes everything, `*.png` only PNGs, `frame_*.png` one numbered run. A name starting with a dot is matched only by a pattern starting with one. Matching is inside the folder: a drive, a leading slash or a '..' segment is refused.

recursive.tooltip: Whether subfolders are listed too. false lists only what sits directly in the folder; true applies the pattern at every depth, so `*.png` also finds 'shot_a/frame_0.png', and every name below the top carries its subfolder.

include.tooltip: What is listed. `files` = files alone, which is what a loop over images wants; `directories` = folders alone, for walking a set of shot folders; `both` = the two together in one order.

sort.tooltip: The order entries come out in. `name` = plain alphabetical, where frame_10 lands before frame_2; `natural` = digits read as numbers, so frame_2 comes first; `modified` = oldest first; `size` = smallest first.

reverse.tooltip: Whether the order is flipped. Off, `modified` gives oldest first and `size` smallest first; on, newest first and largest first, which is how the most recent render is put at index 0.

limit.tooltip: How many entries to keep once they are sorted. 0 = every one; 1 = the first alone; 50 = the first fifty. With sort on `modified` and reverse on, 10 keeps the ten newest files.

output_tooltips: Every entry's full path on one wire, in the chosen order, for Text List Get, Text List Slice and Text List Length. Wire it and count into a For Loop to open one file per iteration.
The same entries named below the folder, as 'frame_0.png' or 'shot_a/frame_0.png', in the same order. Entry 3 here belongs to path 3, so a saved render can carry the name it was made from.
The names, one per line, for reading on a text preview or cutting up again with Text Split to List. Empty when nothing matched.
How many entries the listing holds, which is the length of both lists. Feed it to a For Loop's iterations to walk every one.
WASDirectoryListing.name: WASDirectoryListing
WASDirectoryListing.description: List what is in a folder: every full path on one wire, every name on another, and the count beside them, so a For Loop can take one file per iteration. Files of any kind, picked with a glob such as '*.png' or 'frame_*', optionally descending into subfolders, ordered by name, by number, by date or by size. 'natural' order reads digit runs as numbers, so frame_2 comes before frame_10 rather than after it. 'input', 'output' and 'temp' name ComfyUI's own folders. A folder that is not there stops the prompt; a folder holding nothing the pattern picks answers empty lists and a count of 0.

image.tooltip: Which recently used image to reload. Entries are listed newest last as '.../<folder>/<file>', and read 'No History' until a load or save node has run.

output_tooltips: The reloaded image, as a batch of one, with any transparency discarded.
The file's own name, without the folders leading to it, for reuse as a caption or a save prefix. A missing file reports 'null'.
Image History Loader.name: Image History Loader
Image History Loader.description: Reload one of the images the suite has recently loaded or saved. The menu holds whatever this pack's loading and saving nodes have touched, up to the limit in the pack's config. An entry whose file has since been deleted gives a black 512x512 image, and one in a folder this pack may no longer read stops the prompt with that folder named.

file.tooltip: Which recently used text file to reread. Entries are listed newest last as '.../<folder>/<file>', and read 'No History' until a load or save node has run.

dictionary_name.tooltip: The key the lines are stored under in the dictionary output. Left as '[filename]' it is the part of the file's name before the first dot, so 'animals.txt' becomes 'animals'; anything else is used as the key verbatim.

output_tooltips: The whole file as one string, with comment lines, those starting with '#', removed and the rest kept in order.
The same lines as a list under a single key, so a node that picks a line by index or at random can work through them.
Text File History Loader.name: Text File History Loader
Text File History Loader.description: Reload one of the text files the suite has recently read or written. The menu holds whatever this pack's text loading and saving nodes have touched, up to the limit in the pack's config. A file that has since been deleted gives empty text rather than failing the prompt, and one in a folder this pack may no longer read stops the prompt with that folder named.

images.tooltip: The images to write. Every image in the batch gets its own file, each with the next number in the sequence.

root.tooltip: Which folder the files land in: ComfyUI's own 'output' or 'temp', or any folder added under paths.allow_write in config.yaml, listed by its own name. filename_prefix names the part below it.

filename_prefix.tooltip: The name part of each file, before the number. Tokens are expanded here too, so '[time(%H-%M)]' or a custom token can go in the name rather than the folder. Cleared, the file is just the delimiter and the number.

filename_delimiter.tooltip: What sits between the name and the number: 'ComfyUI_00001.png' with the default, 'ComfyUI-00001.png' with '-'.

filename_number_padding.tooltip: How many digits the number is padded to with leading zeros. 4 gives '_0001', 1 gives '_1'. The count keeps rising past the padding, so too few digits sorts the files oddly rather than failing.

filename_number_start.tooltip: Where the number goes. Off = last, 'ComfyUI_0001.png'; on = first, '0001_ComfyUI.png', which sorts the files by number rather than by name.

extension.tooltip: The file format. `png` is lossless, carries the workflow and takes 16 bits a channel; `exr` holds unclipped linear light at 16 or 32 bit; `jpg` and `jpeg` are small and lossy; `webp` is small and can be either; `tiff` and `bmp` are large and lossless; `gif` is limited to 256 colours.

dpi.tooltip: Print resolution recorded in the file, in dots per inch. It does not resize anything, it only tells a printer or a layout program how large to place the image. Written for png, jpg and jpeg only.

quality.tooltip: How much detail is kept when the format throws some away: 100 is the best the format offers, 80 is a common balance, 1 is heavily degraded. Applies to jpg, jpeg, webp and tiff; png, bmp and gif ignore it.

optimize_image.tooltip: Whether to spend extra time packing the file smaller without changing how it looks. Every format except webp and bmp uses it.

lossless_webp.tooltip: For the webp format only. `on` keeps every pixel exactly and makes a much larger file; `off` compresses it at the quality set above.

overwrite_mode.tooltip: `off` numbers every file, so nothing is ever replaced. `on` drops the number and writes the prefix alone, overwriting the same file on every run, which suits a fixed path an external tool watches.

show_history.tooltip: `off` previews the images this run wrote; `on` previews the files this node has written before instead, newest first, up to the limit in the pack's config.

show_history_by_prefix.tooltip: Narrows the history preview to files in the same folder whose names start with the same prefix. Only has an effect when show_history is on.

embed_workflow.tooltip: Whether to store the workflow inside the file, so dragging the image back into ComfyUI rebuilds the graph. Only png and webp can carry it, and nothing is stored if ComfyUI was started with --disable-metadata.

show_previews.tooltip: Whether the saved images appear on the node. `off` still writes the files and keeps the node small, which suits a long batch.

bit_depth.tooltip: How finely each channel is stored. `8-bit` is 256 levels and is what every format takes; `16-bit` is 65536 and needs `png`, which keeps a gradient banding-free through further grading; `32-bit float` needs `exr` and stores light above 1.0 rather than clipping it. A depth the chosen format cannot hold fails the prompt.

profile.tooltip: A colour profile from Image Load. The images are converted from sRGB into that space and the file is written carrying it, so a photograph goes out tagged the way it came in. Left unconnected, the file is written in sRGB and carries no profile.

output_tooltips: The same images that came in, unchanged, so the node can sit in the middle of a chain instead of ending it.
Full path of every file written this run, in batch order. A file that could not be written is left out of the list.
Image Save.name: Image Save
Image Save.description: Save images with a token-expanded path, a numbered filename and a choice of format. root chooses which folder they land in, and filename_prefix straight into ComfyUI's output directory; a full path writes to that folder instead, as long as it lands inside ComfyUI's output or temp folder, the pack's own folder, or a folder listed under paths.allow_write in config.yaml. Anywhere else is refused, the input folder included.

image.tooltip: Which picture to read. A file in ComfyUI's input folder is listed by name; anything else carries the folder it sits in, as `render.png [output]` or `scratch.png [temp]`. A folder added under paths.allow_read appears under its own name. The button below uploads one into input and selects it.
options: 白鹿、谭松韵今日撞衫，新中式裙子！！_2_胆小面包o_来自小红书网页版.jpg

RGBA.tooltip: `off` discards any transparency and hands on a plain colour image, which is what samplers and most nodes expect; `on` keeps the transparency channel in the image itself. The mask output is produced either way.

filename_text_extension.tooltip: Whether the filename_text output keeps the extension. On = 'cat.png', off = 'cat'. Handy when the name is being reused as a caption or as a save prefix.

colour_space.tooltip: Which colour space the picture comes out in. "the file's own" leaves a tagged file exactly as it was written, for post work that stays there. 'sRGB' is what a sampler, a filter and a LUT expect. The rest, such as 'Adobe RGB (1998)' and 'Display P3', are for a photograph that goes back out in its own space.

icc_mode.tooltip: What to do with the space above. 'convert' changes the numbers so the colour stays put, which is what a photograph wants. 'assign' leaves the numbers alone and says they were in that space all along, which is how an untagged file that is really Display P3 is put right. Ignored for "the file's own".

output_tooltips: The loaded image, as a batch of one.
The image's transparency as a mask, with the transparent parts white and the opaque parts black. An image with no transparency gives an empty 64x64 mask.
The file's own name, without the folders leading to it, for reuse as a caption or a save prefix.

The colour profile the file was tagged with, such as Adobe RGB (1998). Wire it into Image Save to write the result back in that space rather than in sRGB. Empty for a file carrying no profile, which is most of them.
Image Load.name: Image Load
Image Load.description: Load an image chosen from a menu of every picture in ComfyUI's input, output and temp folders, and any folder listed under paths.allow_read in config.yaml. Upload one with the button and it is selected. A file tagged with a colour profile is converted to sRGB as it is read, or kept in its own space, and either way the profile comes out on its own socket. Anything that cannot be read gives a black 512x512 image so the rest of the workflow still runs. A 16-bit PNG loads at full precision, and one marked linear is loaded with no curve applied.

mode.tooltip: Which image of the folder to load. `single_image` takes the one at index; `incremental_image` takes the next one each run and remembers where it stopped, wrapping round; `random` picks one using seed; `all_images` reads every match into image_list and filename_list at once, up to 4096.

seed.tooltip: Chooses the image in `random` mode; the same seed always picks the same one. Ignored by the other two modes.

index.tooltip: Which image to load in `single_image` mode, counting from 0 through the matching files sorted by path. Past the last file the prompt fails. `incremental_image` writes the image it just read back here, so `single_image` carries on from there. The panel says the same, as `index 5 of 0 to 363`.

folder.tooltip: Which folder to read. A bare 'input', 'output' or 'temp' is that folder itself; 'plates/shot_01 [input]' is that folder below it. Any folder added under paths.allow_read in config.yaml is listed under its own name, and so are the folders inside it.

pattern.tooltip: Which files in the folder to consider. '*' takes them all, 'cat_*.png' only those named that way, and '**/*' also descends into subfolders. Files whose format this pack cannot read are skipped whatever the pattern says.

allow_RGBA_output.tooltip: `off` discards any transparency and hands on a plain colour image, which is what samplers and most nodes expect; `on` keeps the transparency channel.

filename_text_extension.tooltip: Whether the filename_text output keeps the extension. On = 'cat.png', off = 'cat'. Handy when the name is being reused as a caption or as a save prefix.

output_tooltips: The single image this run selected, as a batch of one.
That image's own file name, without the folders leading to it, for reuse as a caption or a save prefix.
One image at a time rather than one batch, so a node wired here runs once per image. On `all_images` that is every match in the folder; on the other three modes it is the one image this run selected.
One name per image, in the same order as image_list, with the extension dropped so it can be wired straight into Image Save's filename_prefix. Image Save adds the extension it writes.
Load Image Batch.name: Load Image Batch
Load Image Batch.description: Load one image from a folder by index, in sequence, or at random, or read the whole folder at once. Queue a prompt repeatedly on `incremental_image` to walk a folder image by image; take `all_images` to get every match in one run, as image_list and filename_list. The folder is picked as a root and a path below it, so it always lands inside ComfyUI's input, output or temp folder or one listed under paths.allow_read in config.yaml. A folder that is not there fails the prompt. A 16-bit PNG loads at full precision.

folder.tooltip: Which folder to read. A bare 'input', 'output' or 'temp' is that folder itself; 'plates/shot_01 [input]' is that folder below it. Any folder added under paths.allow_read in config.yaml is listed under its own name, and so are the folders inside it.

pattern.tooltip: Which files to take, as a glob. `*` takes every image in the folder, `frame_*.png` takes one numbered run out of a folder holding several. Matching is inside the folder only.

num_frames.tooltip: How many frames to keep, chosen by the strategy below. `0` = every file in the range, up to the 4096 ceiling; `16` = a short sample. A batch is one tensor, so a long run at full size stops with the count to set rather than running out of memory.

strategy.tooltip: How num_frames are chosen. uniform = evenly spaced; head = first; center = middle; tail = last; random = a seeded pick; every_nth = every nth. Only the chosen files are opened, so sampling a long capture costs the frames you keep rather than all of them.

nth.tooltip: Step between the frames the strategy may choose from. 1 uses every frame; 2 thins to every other one first, so `head` takes the opening of the clip on alternate frames. It applies to every strategy.

seed.tooltip: Seed for random, so a re-run keeps the same frames. Ignored by the other strategies. Any whole number; `0` is as good a seed as any. Left on `fixed`, a re-run is served from the cache instead of the file being read again.

resize_mode.tooltip: How each frame meets the size below, so a folder of mixed sizes still stacks. `fit and pad` keeps the whole frame and pads the rest, `fill and crop` fills the size and trims the overhang, `stretch` distorts to fit, `crop or pad` never resamples.

width.tooltip: Width every frame is brought to. 0 takes the width of the first frame kept, which is what loads a sequence at its own size.

height.tooltip: Height every frame is brought to. 0 takes the height of the first frame kept.

start.tooltip: First file to consider, counting from 0 through the matching files in filename order. Negative counts back from the end.

end.tooltip: Last file to consider, inclusive. -1 is the final file, which is the whole sequence together with a start of 0.

max_size.tooltip: Longest edge the derived size is held to, keeping the aspect. Only read when width and height are 0, which is where a folder of large frames would otherwise fill memory. 0 lifts the cap.

interpolation.tooltip: Resampling filter. `lanczos` is the sharpest for a downscale.

align.tooltip: Which part of a frame survives a crop, and which side carries the wider bar of a pad.

pad_color.tooltip: Fill for space a frame does not cover. Any Pillow colour.

channels.tooltip: Channels the batch carries. `RGBA` keeps the pad transparent.

output_tooltips: The sequence as one batch, in filename order.
How many frames the batch holds once the range and the strategy have been applied.
The filename of each loaded frame, in order, one per line.
The same frames as one image each rather than one batch, so a node wired here runs once per frame. Pair it with filename_list to put every frame through Image Save under its own name.
One name per frame, in the same order as image_list, with the extension dropped so it can be wired straight into Image Save's filename_prefix. Image Save adds the extension it writes.
WASLoadImageSequence.name: WASLoadImageSequence
WASLoadImageSequence.description: Load a numbered sequence from a folder as one batch, in filename order, with the same range and strategy controls the frame samplers use. It takes every frame unless num_frames says otherwise. Load Image Batch beside it serves one frame per run; this serves the run of frames a video pipeline takes, opening only the files it keeps. 16-bit PNGs load and resize at full precision.

file.tooltip: The .txt, .csv, .tsv, .json, .jsonl, .md, .yaml or .yml file to read, tagged with its folder: 'notes.txt [input]', 'notes.txt [output]', or 'notes.txt [prompts]' for a prompts folder under paths.allow_read.

mode.tooltip: What the 'line' output carries. 'file' gives the whole file, every line joined back together, which is what feeds a prompt written across several lines. 'index' gives the single line at 'index', for stepping through a list with a counter. 'random' gives one line drawn by 'seed'. The 'lines' and 'text' outputs are the same in all three.

index.tooltip: Which line 'index' mode takes, counting from 0, so 0 is the first line. -1 is the last line, -2 the one before it. Read only in 'index' mode. What happens past either end is 'out_of_range'.

out_of_range.tooltip: What an index past either end does: 'wrap' starts from the other end, 'clamp' sticks at the first or last line, 'empty' gives nothing, 'error' stops the prompt.

skip_comment_lines.tooltip: Whether lines whose first non-space character is '#' are dropped before anything is counted or numbered. On by default, so the indexes skip notes.

seed.tooltip: Which line 'random' mode draws. The same seed and the same file always give the same line; change it to draw a different one. The seed pins a position rather than a line, so adding or removing a line in the file, or changing skip_comment_lines, makes the same seed produce different text. Read only in 'random' mode.

output_tooltips: What the chosen mode selected: the whole file on 'file', one line on 'index' and 'random'. Empty when the file could not be read or holds no line to select.
Every line of the file on one wire, for Text List Slice, Text List Get, Text List Length and Text List to Strings. Comment lines are absent while skip_comment_lines is on.
The whole file as one string, the same lines joined with line breaks, whatever the mode. Wire this into Text Random Line or Text Find and Replace to work on the file as a whole.
How many lines the file has, after comment lines are dropped. 0 for an empty file and for one that could not be read.

Which line number the 'line' output really came from, after wrapping or clamping, counting from 0. -1 in 'file' mode and whenever no single line was selected. Worth watching when a counter drives the index or a seed drives the draw.
WASLoadTextLine.name: WASLoadTextLine
WASLoadTextLine.description: Read a text file picked from a menu: the whole file, the line at an index, or a line drawn from a seed, with every line also given as a list. The menu lists the text files in ComfyUI's input and output folders, subfolders included, and in every folder under paths.allow_read in config.yaml, each tagged with its folder's name. A folder added there appears after a ComfyUI restart and a page reload. A file since deleted or renamed gives empty text and a line in the log.

file.tooltip: Which video to read. Each entry carries the folder it sits in: `clip.mp4 [input]`, `render.mp4 [output]`, `scratch.mp4 [temp]`. The button below uploads one into input and selects it, and the player shows what is selected.

num_frames.tooltip: How many frames to keep, chosen by the strategy below. `0` = the whole clip, up to the 4096 ceiling; `16` = a short sample. A batch is one tensor, so a long clip at full size stops with the count to set rather than running out of memory.

strategy.tooltip: How num_frames are chosen. uniform = evenly spaced; head = first; center = middle; tail = last; random = a seeded pick; every_nth = every nth. uniform gives a contact sheet of a whole clip, head gives a run that plays.

nth.tooltip: Step between the frames the strategy may choose from. 1 uses every frame; 2 thins to every other one first, so `head` takes the opening of the clip on alternate frames. It applies to every strategy.

seed.tooltip: Seed for random, so a re-run keeps the same frames. Ignored by the other strategies. Any whole number; `0` is as good a seed as any. Left on `fixed`, a re-run is served from the cache instead of the file being read again.

target_fps.tooltip: Rate the frames come out at. 0 keeps the file's own. A lower rate drops frames and a higher one repeats them, so the clip runs for the same time either way. Set it to match a model that wants 8 or 16 fps.

resize_mode.tooltip: How each frame meets the size below. `fit and pad` keeps the whole frame and pads the rest, `fill and crop` fills the size and trims the overhang, `stretch` distorts to fit, `crop or pad` never resamples.

width.tooltip: Width every frame is brought to. 0 takes the width the file was encoded at, which is what loads a clip at its own size.

height.tooltip: Height every frame is brought to. 0 takes the height the file was encoded at.

start.tooltip: First frame to consider, counting from 0 through the file's own frames. Negative counts back from the end, so -60 starts sixty frames before it.

end.tooltip: Last frame to consider, inclusive. -1 is the final frame, which is the whole clip together with a start of 0.

max_size.tooltip: Longest edge the derived size is held to, keeping the aspect. Only read when width and height are 0, which is where a 4K clip would otherwise fill memory. 0 lifts the cap.

interpolation.tooltip: Resampling filter. `lanczos` is the sharpest for a downscale.

align.tooltip: Which part of a frame survives a crop, and which side carries the wider bar of a pad.

pad_color.tooltip: Fill for space a frame does not cover. Any Pillow colour.

channels.tooltip: Channels the image batch carries. `RGBA` keeps the pad transparent. The video output is always colour, since a video carries no transparency.

output_tooltips: The frames that were kept, with their sound, as a video at the rate below. Wire it into Save Video, or into any node taking a VIDEO.
The same frames as one image batch, in playback order, every one at the same size.
The sound playing under the frames that were kept, from where they start and for as long as they run. Empty when the file is silent, so read has_audio before wiring this into a save node.

What this read measured: the rate, the frame count, the size, the duration, the bit depth and whether there is sound, beside the same figures for the file itself. Wire it into Video Metadata to read any of them as a number.
WASLoadVideo.name: WASLoadVideo
WASLoadVideo.description: Load a video from ComfyUI's input folder and hand on everything in it at once: the video itself, its frames as an image batch, its sound, and how long it is. Upload a file with the button on the node and play it back there. Frames are chosen with the same range and strategy controls the frame samplers use, and brought to one size the same way the image loaders do it. 16 frames are taken unless told otherwise, since a clip can hold thousands and a batch is one tensor in memory.

cache.tooltip: Which frame cache to read, as `frame_cache/scene_00001/cache.wasframes [output]`. A cache in temp is gone after a restart.

delete_after_save.tooltip: `true` = the cache is deleted once a save has written all of it; `false` = it is kept for the next save.

output_tooltips: The cached clip, read from disk by Save Video a frame at a time.
Frames the cache holds.
Its frames per second.
WASLoadVideoCache.name: WASLoadVideoCache
WASLoadVideoCache.description: Pick a frame cache written by Video Cache or H3 Decode Video and use it as a clip again, to save it in another format or carry on with it after a restart, without rendering it again.

file.tooltip: Which video to read, from ComfyUI's input folder. The button below uploads one and selects it, and the player shows what is selected.

num_frames.tooltip: How many frames to keep, chosen by the strategy below. `0` = the whole clip, up to the 4096 ceiling; `16` = a short sample. A batch is one tensor, so a long clip at full size stops with the count to set rather than running out of memory.

strategy.tooltip: How num_frames are chosen. uniform = evenly spaced; head = first; center = middle; tail = last; random = a seeded pick; every_nth = every nth. uniform gives a contact sheet of a whole clip, head gives a run that plays.

nth.tooltip: Step between the frames the strategy may choose from. 1 uses every frame; 2 thins to every other one first, so `head` takes the opening of the clip on alternate frames. It applies to every strategy.

seed.tooltip: Seed for random, so a re-run keeps the same frames. Ignored by the other strategies. Any whole number; `0` is as good a seed as any. Left on `fixed`, a re-run is served from the cache instead of the file being read again.

target_fps.tooltip: Rate the frames come out at. 0 keeps the file's own. A lower rate drops frames and a higher one repeats them, so the clip runs for the same time either way. Set it to match a model that wants 8 or 16 fps.

resize_mode.tooltip: How each frame meets the size below. `fit and pad` keeps the whole frame and pads the rest, `fill and crop` fills the size and trims the overhang, `stretch` distorts to fit, `crop or pad` never resamples.

width.tooltip: Width every frame is brought to. 0 takes the width the file was encoded at, which is what loads a clip at its own size.

height.tooltip: Height every frame is brought to. 0 takes the height the file was encoded at.

start.tooltip: First frame to consider, counting from 0 through the file's own frames. Negative counts back from the end, so -60 starts sixty frames before it.

end.tooltip: Last frame to consider, inclusive. -1 is the final frame, which is the whole clip together with a start of 0.

max_size.tooltip: Longest edge the derived size is held to, keeping the aspect. Only read when width and height are 0, which is where a 4K clip would otherwise fill memory. 0 lifts the cap.

interpolation.tooltip: Resampling filter. `lanczos` is the sharpest for a downscale.

align.tooltip: Which part of a frame survives a crop, and which side carries the wider bar of a pad.

pad_color.tooltip: Fill for space a frame does not cover. Any Pillow colour.

channels.tooltip: Channels the image batch carries. `RGBA` keeps the pad transparent. The video output is always colour, since a video carries no transparency.

output_tooltips: The frames that were kept, with their sound, as a video at the rate below. Wire it into Save Video, or into any node taking a VIDEO.
The same frames as one image batch, in playback order, every one at the same size.
The sound playing under the frames that were kept, from where they start and for as long as they run. Empty when the file is silent, so read has_audio before wiring this into a save node.

What this read measured: the rate, the frame count, the size, the duration, the bit depth and whether there is sound, beside the same figures for the file itself. Wire it into Video Metadata to read any of them as a number.
WASLoadVideoUpload.name: WASLoadVideoUpload
WASLoadVideoUpload.description: Load a video and hand on everything in it at once: the video itself, its frames as an image batch, its sound, and how long it is. Upload a file with the button on the node and play it back there. Frames are chosen and sized exactly as Load Video beside it does them, 16 of them unless told otherwise.

path.tooltip: The file or folder to look for, such as 'C:/renders/frame_0001.png', or a path relative to the folder ComfyUI was started in. Nothing is opened, read or written; the path is only asked about.

output_tooltips: true when something is at that path. A folder counts, and so does a file of 0 bytes. false when nothing is there, and false for a path outside the folders this pack may read.
true only for an ordinary file. false for a folder and false when nothing is there, so pair it with exists to tell 'a folder is at that path' from 'nothing is'.
true only for a folder. false for a file and false when nothing is there. Wire it to a switch that picks between loading a whole folder and loading one file.
Bytes the file holds. 0 for a folder, 0 when nothing is there, and 0 for an empty file, so 'size_bytes > 0' is the test for a render that finished writing rather than one cut off at the start.
When it last changed, in seconds since 1970, as 1755864000.0. 0.0 when nothing is there. Feed two of these to Compare to tell which of a source and a cache is the newer.
The same moment in local time, as '2026-08-22 11:57:03'. Empty when nothing is there. For reading and for naming a file; compare modified_epoch instead of this.

The absolute path that was probed. For a path outside the folders this pack may read, nothing is probed and this carries the refusal instead, naming every permitted folder and the config key that would allow it.
WASPathExists.name: WASPathExists
WASPathExists.description: Ask whether a file or folder is already on disk before anything reads or writes it, and get back what is there: file or folder, how many bytes, and when it last changed. A folder batch can skip the frames it has already rendered, and a cache can be compared against the file it was built from. A path outside the folders this pack may read is answered as not existing, with the refusal on 'resolved', so a probe never stops the prompt.

images.tooltip: The frames of the animation, in order.

root.tooltip: Which folder the file lands in: ComfyUI's own 'output' or 'temp', or any folder added under paths.allow_write in config.yaml.

filename_prefix.tooltip: The file's name before its number, such as `renders/walk` for a subfolder.

fps.tooltip: Frames per second. `24` plays as film, `6` as a slow loop.
