output_tooltips: The model for the sampler that refines the latent.
How many cuts the latent records; where there are several time windows, none crosses one.
WASH3Tiles.name: WASH3Tiles
WASH3Tiles.description: Run every MiniMax H3 model call in overlapping tiles across the frame and overlapping windows along the clip, blended where they meet at each step so the tiles stay one clip. Any sampler then refines a long or upscaled H3 latent in tiles that each fit the card, run as H3 Low VRAM runs them. Upscale the latent first, or decode, upscale and encode, and sample it at a partial denoise. Wire the clip's latent as well and, where it takes several time windows, each one stays inside one scene, so no blend crosses a cut.

model.tooltip: The diffusion model every cycle samples with, unless secondary_model takes over partway through.

seed.tooltip: Seed for the noise. Every cycle uses this same seed, so the whole run is repeatable; change it for a different image. Any whole number; `0` is as good a seed as any.

steps.tooltip: Sampling steps on the first cycle. More steps take longer and resolve more detail, with little to gain past about 30 for most models. Turning steps_scaling on changes this figure on later cycles.

cfg.tooltip: How closely the image is held to the prompt. Around 7-8 suits most models; lower is looser and softer, much higher tends to burn contrast and flatten detail.

sampler_name.tooltip: The sampling algorithm. 'euler' is the plain, predictable choice; the 'ancestral' and 'sde' variants add fresh noise as they go and keep changing the image at high step counts; the 'dpmpp' family converges in fewer steps. The list is whatever this ComfyUI offers.

scheduler.tooltip: How the noise level is stepped down over the run. 'normal' and 'karras' are the usual choices, karras spending more steps at low noise where fine detail is decided. The list is whatever this ComfyUI offers.

positive.tooltip: Encoded prompt describing what the image should contain.

negative.tooltip: Encoded prompt describing what to keep out of the image.

latent_image.tooltip: The latent the first cycle works on: an empty one to generate from scratch, or an encoded image to work up from. Its size sets where the enlargement starts.

tiled_vae.tooltip: `enable` converts between latent and pixels a tile at a time, which needs far less VRAM at large sizes and can leave faint seams. Only matters when latent_upscale is `disable`, since that is the only path that goes through pixels.

latent_upscale.tooltip: How the enlargement between cycles is done. `disable` takes the slower, sharper route through pixels, using vae, upscale_model, processor_model and scale_sampling. Any other entry stays in latent space and is much faster, ignoring all four; `nearest-exact` is the blockiest, `bilinear` and `bicubic` smoother, `area` averages, and `bislerp` is a blend built for latents.

upscale_factor.tooltip: Total enlargement across the whole run, not per cycle: 2.0 means the result is twice the size it started at, and the cycles share that growth evenly between them.

upscale_cycles.tooltip: How many sample passes to run. Enlargement happens between passes, so 2 grows once and 4 grows three times in smaller jumps, which is gentler but slower. Capped at steps, since a pass needs at least one step.

starting_denoise.tooltip: How much of the first pass is redrawn. 1.0 ignores latent_image's content and generates from noise; around 0.5 keeps its composition and changes the detail; 0.0 changes nothing.

cycle_denoise.tooltip: How much every pass after the first redraws. This is what keeps the enlarged image recognisable: 0.5 refines it, and much above that starts inventing new content at each size.

scale_denoise.tooltip: `enable` halves cycle_denoise again on each pass after the second, so later passes only polish; denoise_cutoff sets how low it may go. `disable` uses cycle_denoise unchanged on every pass.

scale_sampling.tooltip: Which filter resizes the decoded picture on the pixel-space route. `lanczos` and `bicubic` are the sharpest, `bilinear` softer, `nearest` blocky. Ignored unless latent_upscale is `disable`.

vae.tooltip: The VAE used to decode to pixels and encode back between cycles. Required even when latent_upscale keeps the work in latent space and nothing is decoded.

secondary_model.tooltip: A second diffusion model to hand the later cycles to, so one model lays out the image and another finishes it. Disconnected, one model does the whole run.

secondary_start_cycle.tooltip: Which pass secondary_model takes over on, counting from 1, so 2 hands over straight after the first. That pass also uses cycle_denoise rather than any scaled-down value.

upscale_model.tooltip: An upscale model such as ESRGAN to do the enlarging, which recovers far more detail than a plain resize. Its result is fitted to the target size, rounded to a multiple of 32. Disconnected, the picture is simply resampled. Ignored unless latent_upscale is `disable`.

processor_model.tooltip: An upscale model run before the enlargement and shrunk straight back to the size it started at, so it cleans up artefacts and restores detail without changing the size. Ignored unless latent_upscale is `disable`.

pos_additive.tooltip: A second positive prompt mixed into the first a little more, or a little less, on every cycle, a way to steer the image somewhere new as it grows. Disconnected, the positive prompt stays as it is.

neg_additive.tooltip: A second negative prompt mixed into the first a little more, or a little less, on every cycle. Disconnected, the negative prompt stays as it is.

pos_add_mode.tooltip: Which way pos_add_strength moves between cycles: `increment` doubles it each pass, so pos_additive takes over gradually; `decrement` halves it, so its influence fades out. Only used when pos_add_strength_scaling is enabled.

pos_add_strength.tooltip: How much of pos_additive is mixed in on the first cycle. 0.25 is a quarter of the way towards it, 1.0 replaces the positive prompt outright.

pos_add_strength_scaling.tooltip: `enable` lets pos_add_mode change the strength from cycle to cycle. `disable` holds pos_add_strength steady for the whole run.

pos_add_strength_cutoff.tooltip: The limit the scaled strength is held to: a ceiling while incrementing, a floor while decrementing. At the default of 2.0 in increment mode the strength is effectively unbounded, since 1.0 already means full replacement.

neg_add_mode.tooltip: Which way neg_add_strength moves between cycles: `increment` doubles it each pass, `decrement` halves it. Only used when neg_add_strength_scaling is enabled.

neg_add_strength.tooltip: How much of neg_additive is mixed in on the first cycle. 0.25 is a quarter of the way towards it, 1.0 replaces the negative prompt outright.

neg_add_strength_scaling.tooltip: `enable` lets neg_add_mode change the strength from cycle to cycle. `disable` holds neg_add_strength steady for the whole run.

neg_add_strength_cutoff.tooltip: The limit the scaled strength is held to: a ceiling while incrementing, a floor while decrementing.

sharpen_strength.tooltip: How hard to sharpen the enlarged picture before it is encoded again. 0.0 skips sharpening entirely; around 1.0 counteracts the softness of a resize; far above that leaves halos. Ignored unless latent_upscale is `disable`.

sharpen_radius.tooltip: How wide the sharpening reaches, in pixels. Small values pick out fine texture, large ones lift broad edges and coarsen the picture. Only used when sharpen_strength is above 0.

steps_scaling.tooltip: `enable` changes the step count on every pass after the first, by steps_scaling_value and in the direction steps_control names. `disable` keeps steps the same throughout.

steps_control.tooltip: Which way the step count moves. `decrement` spends fewer steps on each larger pass, which is the cheaper choice since low-denoise passes need fewer; `increment` spends more.

steps_scaling_value.tooltip: How many steps are added or taken away on each pass after the first. Only used when steps_scaling is enabled.

steps_cutoff.tooltip: The step count the scaling is not allowed past: a ceiling while incrementing, a floor while decrementing. At the default of 20, with steps also 20 and steps_control on `decrement`, the count never moves.

denoise_cutoff.tooltip: The lowest denoise the halving under scale_denoise may reach, so later passes still do some work. Ignored when scale_denoise is disabled.

output_tooltips: The latent after the final pass, at the full enlarged size. Decode it with a VAE Decode to see the picture.
KSampler Cycle.name: KSampler Cycle
KSampler Cycle.description: Sample a latent over several cycles, enlarging it between passes by an even share of upscale_factor. Scaling runs in latent space, or through a VAE round trip with an optional upscale model and unsharp sharpening.

pattern.tooltip: Which mask shapes the draw. `white_noise` is one value per latent element; `pink_noise`, `brown_noise` and `perlin` spread over larger areas; `checker`, `bayer` and `tile_lines` repeat. Affine Options carries each pattern's own settings.

noise_seed.tooltip: The seed the draw and the mask are both taken from, as `0` or `12345`. One seed reproduces a clip exactly.

max_scale.tooltip: What the draw is multiplied by where the mask is white. 1.0 leaves the draw alone, 1.1 lifts it a tenth, 0.5 halves it. Away from the mask the draw is untouched.

max_bias.tooltip: What is added where the mask is white. 0.0 adds nothing, 0.05 is a faint lift, 0.5 prints the pattern into the draw.

clamp_sigma.tooltip: Where the draw is cut off, in standard deviations. 0.0 leaves it uncut. 3.0 cuts the furthest 0.3 percent of values.

temporal_mode.tooltip: How a video latent's mask varies over time. 'static' = one mask on every frame, in the same place all clip. 'per_frame' = an unrelated mask each frame. 'drift' = one mask slid across the frame, set by drift_speed, drift_angle_deg and drift_renew on Affine Options. The content-aware patterns ignore this, and so does an image latent.

streams.tooltip: Which streams of a packed audio and video latent the affine reaches. 'video' = stream 0, 'audio' = the rest, 'both' = all of them. An ordinary latent has only a video stream, so 'audio' does nothing to it.

normalize.tooltip: `true` returns the draw at a spread of 1.0, which is the magnitude a sampler's schedule is built for. `false` returns whatever max_scale and max_bias worked out to.

affine_options.tooltip: Pattern parameters and mask shaping from an Affine Options node. Leave it unwired and every value takes its default. A pattern set there wins over the pattern widget.

output_tooltips: The starting noise, for the noise socket of Sampler Custom Advanced or Custom Sampler Affine Advanced.
WASAffinePatternNoise.name: WASAffinePatternNoise
WASAffinePatternNoise.description: Starting noise with an affine mask laid over it: the draw is multiplied by max_scale and offset by max_bias wherever the pattern is white, so the noise carries the pattern's structure instead of being flat. Wire it into the noise socket of any custom sampler in place of RandomNoise. The four patterns read off a picture are not offered, since a starting draw has no picture to read.

base_sampler.tooltip: The solver each segment runs. A solver that carries state between steps starts that state again at every transition, so the simpler ones behave most predictably here.

scales.tooltip: Fractions of the full resolution to sample at, increasing, ending at 1.0. `0.5,1.0` starts at half size and grows once. A single `1.0` disables growth and samples normally throughout.

transform.tooltip: The basis the latent grows in. `dct` and `fft` handle any ratio between scales; `dwt` is cheaper but only ever doubles, so every step in the list has to be exactly twice the one before it.

delta.tooltip: How much leftover noise counts as burying a frequency. Larger values hold the small grid for more steps, saving more but leaving less of the schedule to resolve detail in. The default is conservative: it grows after about a sixth of the steps.

amplitude.tooltip: The A of the model's power spectrum, eg 203.6 for FLUX.1-dev. Only meaningful alongside delta: a measured A runs larger than a published one, so take both from the same place.

beta.tooltip: How fast the model's spectrum falls away with frequency. Unlike the amplitude this is a property of the model rather than of the scale its latents happen to be in, so a measured one is directly comparable to a published one. The default belongs to FLUX.1-dev.

seed.tooltip: Seeds the noise that fills the frequencies each transition adds. Changing it varies the fine detail without moving the composition. Any whole number; `0` is as good a seed as any.

manual_sigmas.tooltip: Sigmas to grow at, one per transition, decreasing. Leave this empty to have them worked out from the amplitude and beta instead, which is the usual way round. Setting them ignores delta, amplitude and beta.

output_tooltips: Feeds the SAMPLER socket of SamplerCustom.
WASSpeedSampler.name: WASSpeedSampler
WASSpeedSampler.description: Sample the early steps at a reduced resolution and grow the latent partway through, in a spectral basis so the detail that appears is resolved rather than interpolated. Needs a flow-matching model, and the spectrum values it schedules from should be measured with Latent Power Spectrum.

noise_seed.tooltip: The seed the noise field is drawn from, as `0` or `12345`. The same seed and hold reproduce a clip exactly.

hold.tooltip: How many latent frames the noise pattern carries over. 0.0 draws ordinary noise and matches RandomNoise exactly. Higher values cut the frame-to-frame change: 2.0 to 0.63 of ordinary noise, 8.0 to 0.34, 25.0 to 0.20, 64.0 to 0.12, 128.0 to 0.09. One latent frame is about 3.4 output frames on MiniMax H3, 4 on Wan and 8 on LTX.

output_tooltips: The starting noise, for the noise socket of Sampler Custom Advanced or Custom Sampler Affine Advanced.
WASTemporalNoiseHold.name: WASTemporalNoiseHold
WASTemporalNoiseHold.description: Starting noise whose pattern carries over from one video frame to the next instead of being redrawn each time. The further it carries, the denser and more detailed the scene comes back. Wire it into the noise socket of any custom sampler in place of RandomNoise. Only the first draw is shaped, so a sampler that draws fresh noise at every step overwrites it: the ancestral and SDE families, and any sampler whose eta is above 0, which several default to. euler, heun, dpm_2, dpmpp_2m and the ode variants keep it.

dictionary_text.tooltip: Dictionary literal; STRING. Single or double quotes both work. Eg: {'subject': 'a cat'}

output_tooltips: The dictionary the text described, for the other DICT nodes.
Text Dictionary Convert.name: Text Dictionary Convert
Text Dictionary Convert.description: Convert text holding a dictionary literal into a dictionary. The text is read with ast.literal_eval, which accepts single quotes as well as JSON's double quotes and executes nothing.

default_value.tooltip: Emitted when the dictionary has no such key. Left empty, a missing key gives an empty string rather than failing the prompt.

output_tooltips: The entry's value as text. A value that is a list or a number is rendered the way python prints it, so a list arrives as ['a', 'b'].

Text Dictionary Get.description: Look up a key in a dictionary and emit its value as text. A key that is not in the dictionary emits the default value.

Text Dictionary New.name: Text Dictionary New
Text Dictionary New.description: Build a DICT from up to 24 key/value pairs. A value can be a STRING, or a LIST of alternatives for Text Find and Replace by Dictionary to draw from. Empty keys are skipped.

dictionary.tooltip: The dictionary to write out as text.

output_tooltips: The dictionary written out on one line, for example {'subject': 'a cat'}. Useful for a preview or a saved text file, and Text Dictionary Convert reads it back.
Text Dictionary To Text.name: Text Dictionary To Text
Text Dictionary To Text.description: Render a dictionary as text. The result uses single quotes and reads back through Text Dictionary Convert.

dictionary_b.tooltip: Merged over dictionary_a, so a key in both takes this one's value.

dictionary_c.tooltip: Merged over the first two. Unconnected, it contributes nothing.

Text Dictionary Update.name: Text Dictionary Update
Text Dictionary Update.description: Merge two to 24 dictionaries into one. Keys present in more than one input take the value of the last input that carries them.

dictionary.tooltip: The dictionary whose entries are wanted, keys and values both.

sort.tooltip: Order both lists come out in. `none` = the order the entries were added; `key` = A to Z by name; `value` = A to Z by the value as text. Case is ignored, so 'Apple' sits beside 'apple', and digits sort as text: '10' before '9'.

output_tooltips: The entry names on one wire, such as ['subject', 'style']. Feed it to Text List Get with a For Loop's index to read one name per iteration.
What each name is stored against, in step with keys. An entry holding several alternatives stays a list, so ['a cat', 'a wolf'] arrives whole rather than as writing.

Every entry written as `subject: a cat`, one to a line. For a preview, a caption or a saved text file. A value carrying line breaks of its own spans several lines. An empty dictionary gives an empty string.
How many entries the dictionary holds, 0 when it holds none. Feed it to a For Loop's iteration count to run the graph once per entry.
WASTextDictionaryItems.name: WASTextDictionaryItems
WASTextDictionaryItems.description: Open a dictionary into two lists that line up: the keys, and their values. Entry 0 of one belongs with entry 0 of the other, so a For Loop stepping one index through both reads a key and its value together. The entries also come out written as text, and counted for the loop to run on.

clip.tooltip: A CLIP holding a language model, such as Qwen3 4B from Load CLIP with type `lumina2`, or Gemma 3 with type `ltxv`.

prompt.tooltip: What to ask the model, such as `Describe a lighthouse on a stormy night.`

max_length.tooltip: The most tokens to write. A token is about three quarters of a word, so `512` is about 380 words.

sampling_mode.tooltip: `on` draws each token at random within the limits below. `off` always takes the likeliest token and writes the same text every time.

temperature.tooltip: How adventurous each pick is. `0.7` is balanced, `0.2` stays close to the likeliest words, `1.2` wanders.

top_k.tooltip: Pick only among this many likeliest tokens. `0` turns the limit off.

top_p.tooltip: Pick only among the likeliest tokens whose chances add up to this. `1.0` turns it off.

min_p.tooltip: Drop any token less likely than this fraction of the likeliest one. `0` turns it off.

repetition_penalty.tooltip: Above `1.0` makes a token already used less likely again. `1.0` turns it off.

seed.tooltip: The same seed with the same settings writes the same text.

presence_penalty.tooltip: Subtracted from every token already used. `0` turns it off, `0.5` pushes toward new words.

image.tooltip: A picture to ask about, for a model that reads images such as Qwen 2.5 VL or Gemma 3.

video.tooltip: Video frames as an image batch, read as 24 fps and sampled at 1 fps.

audio.tooltip: Sound to ask about, for a model that hears it.

thinking.tooltip: `true` lets a model that reasons, such as Qwen3, think before answering.

use_default_template.tooltip: `true` wraps the prompt in the model's own chat template and system prompt.

mtp.tooltip: Multi-token prediction for a checkpoint carrying those heads. `auto` picks the draft depth, `2` to `5` fixes it, `off` turns it off.

fast_decode.tooltip: `true` decodes on the fixed cache graph path where the model allows it; `false` runs exactly as core Generate Text.

output_tooltips: What the model wrote, special tokens removed.
WASFastGenerateText.name: WASFastGenerateText
WASFastGenerateText.description: Write text with the language model inside a loaded CLIP, as core Generate Text does, several times faster on the models core leaves on its slow decode. It switches the model onto ComfyUI's own fixed cache and graph captured decode for the run and back afterwards. The panel shows tokens per second and which decode ran.

text_list.tooltip: The list to read from, such as the LIST output of Text Split to List, Text List or Text Dictionary Keys.

index.tooltip: Which entry to take, counting from 0. -1 is the last entry, -2 the one before it. Wire a Number Counter in to step through the list one entry per run. A decimal value is cut down to a whole number.

out_of_range.tooltip: What an index past the end does: `wrap` counts round again, `clamp` sticks at the first or last entry, `empty` returns nothing, `error` stops the prompt.

WASTextListGet.name: WASTextListGet
WASTextListGet.description: Read one entry out of a list by position. Negative counts from the end, and an index past either end wraps, clamps, comes back empty or stops, whichever is chosen. `wrap` counts round again, so index 5 of a 3-entry list is entry 2, which is what cycles a list forever from a counter that only climbs. `error` suits a workflow where a missing entry means something is wrong upstream.

text_list.tooltip: The list to count, such as the LIST output of Text Split to List, Text List, Text Dictionary Keys or Image Color Palette.

WASTextListLength.name: WASTextListLength
WASTextListLength.description: Count the entries in a list, as a NUMBER, an INT and a FLOAT. Also reports whether the list is empty, for a switch that has to handle that case.

text_list.tooltip: The list to take from, such as the lines output of Load Text Line or the LIST output of Text Split to List, Text List or Text Dictionary Keys.

start.tooltip: The first entry taken, counting from 0, and it is taken. -1 is the last entry, -2 the one before it. A start before the beginning of the list begins at the first entry.

end.tooltip: The last entry taken, and it is taken as well: start 9 and end 19 give 11 entries, the 10th to the 20th. -1 is the last entry.

step.tooltip: How far to move between entries taken. 1 takes every entry, 2 takes every second one starting at start, 3 every third. The last entry is taken only when the stepping lands on it.

output_tooltips: The entries taken, on one wire, for Text List Get, Text List Concatenate and Text List to Text.

The same entries as a STRING list. Because this is a list, a node reading it runs once per entry and produces one result per entry, wire it into a sampler's prompt to render every line of a range in turn. An entry that is not text is converted to it.
How many entries the range took.
WASTextListSlice.name: WASTextListSlice
WASTextListSlice.description: Take a run of entries out of a list, from one position to another with both ends included, optionally every second or third one. The run comes out twice: as one LIST, and as a STRING list that runs everything downstream once per entry. An end of -1, the default, takes everything from start onwards, and an end past the last entry stops there. An end before start selects nothing and stops the prompt, since the graph below cannot be run zero times.

text_list.tooltip: The list to read. Entries may be numbers already or text holding one; surrounding space, a leading + or - and a decimal point are all read, so '  -1.5 ' arrives as -1.5.

unreadable.tooltip: What an entry that is not a number does. `skip` leaves it out, `zero` keeps the position and puts 0 there, and `error` stops the prompt.

round_to_int.tooltip: Whether the INT socket rounds to the nearest whole number instead of cutting the decimal off. Off, 1.9 arrives as 1; on, it arrives as 2. The NUMBER and FLOAT sockets keep the decimal either way.

output_tooltips: One NUMBER per entry, for the maths and counter nodes. A node reading this runs once per value. If nothing in the list reads as a number the prompt stops, because a graph cannot be run zero times, set unreadable to `zero` to keep a value in every position.
The same values as decimals, one per run.
The same values as whole numbers, one per run, for a step count or a seed.
How many values came through, which is how many times the graph below this node runs.
WASTextListToNumbers.name: WASTextListToNumbers
WASTextListToNumbers.description: Read a LIST as numbers and emit them on the NUMBER, FLOAT and INT sockets as lists, so every node downstream runs once per value. `skip` suits a column with a heading on the first line, `zero` a schedule where entry 7 has to stay entry 7, and `error` names the entry it stopped on. An entry reading as nan or as infinity takes the same route as an unreadable one.

text_list.tooltip: The list to unpack. Any LIST output does: Text Split to List, Text List, Text Dictionary Keys, Image Color Palette.

remove_empty.tooltip: Whether entries holding nothing are dropped before the list is handed on. Each empty entry would otherwise cost a full run of everything downstream to produce a result from an empty prompt.

output_tooltips: The entries, one per run. A node reading this executes once for each of them, so a list of six prompts renders six images. An empty list stops the prompt, because a graph cannot be run zero times.
How many entries were handed on, which is how many times the graph below this node runs.
WASTextListToStrings.name: WASTextListToStrings
WASTextListToStrings.description: Turn a LIST into a STRING list, which runs every node downstream once per entry. The way to feed a list into nodes that take plain text.

delimiter.tooltip: Placed between the entries. The default ', ' builds a comma-separated prompt; type \n to put each entry on its own line; leave it empty to run them together with nothing between.

text_list.tooltip: The list to flatten, for example the lines of a file from Text Load Line From File or the entries of Text List. Every entry has to be text; a list holding a number fails the prompt.

output_tooltips: The list's entries as one string, separated by the delimiter.
Text List to Text.name: Text List to Text
Text List to Text.description: Join a list into one string, separated by the delimiter. Type \n as the delimiter to join with newlines.

text.tooltip: The text to cut up, as `cat, forest, sunset`. Typed here, or wired in from any node with a text output, such as a prompt built by Text Concatenate.

split_by.tooltip: Where the cuts go. `delimiter` and `regex` read the delimiter field; `lines` cuts on line breaks, `whitespace` on runs of space, `characters` on every character.

delimiter.tooltip: What to cut on, read only by `delimiter` and `regex`. Type \n for a line break or \t for a tab. An unreadable regular expression stops with the error the pattern produced, naming the position in it that failed.

trim_whitespace.tooltip: Whether each piece has its surrounding space removed. On, 'a, b, c' gives 'a', 'b', 'c'; off it gives 'a', ' b', ' c', and the leading spaces travel into whatever reads the list.

remove_empty.tooltip: Whether pieces holding nothing are dropped. Two delimiters in a row produce an empty piece, which is what a trailing comma on a prompt leaves behind. Turn this off when the position of every entry matters and an empty slot has to stay a slot.

output_tooltips: Every piece on one wire, for Text List Get, Text List Concatenate and Text List to Text.

The same pieces as a STRING list. Because this is a list, a node reading it runs once per piece and produces one result per piece, wire it into a sampler's prompt to render every entry in turn. Text that splits into nothing stops the prompt, because a graph cannot be run zero times.
How many pieces the split produced.
WASTextSplitToList.name: WASTextSplitToList
WASTextSplitToList.description: Split text into a list, on a delimiter, on line breaks, on whitespace or on a regular expression. The pieces come out twice: as one LIST, and as a STRING list that runs everything downstream once per piece. `delimiter` cuts on the exact text in the delimiter field, which is how a comma-separated prompt becomes one entry per tag, while `regex` reads that field as a pattern, so `[,;]` cuts on either mark. `characters` ignores the delimiter field.

text.tooltip: The prompt, in any of three markups. __term__ draws a phrase from the terminology pantry or a line from a wildcard file; <a|b|c> picks one of the alternatives; $|a stormy sky|$ captures the phrase as $1 so it can be repeated by number later in the prompt.

mode.tooltip: What __terms__ are replaced with. `Noodle Soup Prompts` draws from the shared terminology pantry, downloaded once and then cached. `Wildcards` draws a random line from the matching file in the wildcards directory, where a subfolder is part of the name, so __animals/birds__ reads animals/birds.txt. `none` leaves __terms__ alone, for a prompt that only uses the groups and variables below.

noodle_key.tooltip: The marker put either side of a term to flag it for replacement. With the default '__', __animals__ is replaced and plain animals is not.

seed.tooltip: Which words get drawn. Any value other than 0 makes the whole parse repeatable, so the same seed and the same prompt always give the same text. 0 is the exception the term draw treats as unseeded, so __terms__ come out different every run while the <a|b|c> groups stay fixed.

dynamic_prompts.tooltip: Whether <a|b|c> groups are resolved to one of their options. Turn it off to keep the brackets in the text, which is what a prompt being passed on to another parser needs.

prompt_variables.tooltip: Whether $|phrase|$ captures are expanded. A capture is numbered in the order it appears and replaced by $1, $2 and so on, and every reference to that number anywhere in the prompt then becomes the phrase, which is how one long description is written once and repeated.

output_tooltips: The finished prompt, with every enabled markup expanded. Worth saving beside the image with Text Save, since a new seed produces different words.
The prompt exactly as it arrived, markup and all.
WASPromptParse.name: WASPromptParse
WASPromptParse.description: Expand __terms__, <a|b|c> groups and $|phrase|$ variables and return the finished text. Every markup CLIPTextEncode (NSP) understands, stopping at the string so it can be saved, split or encoded elsewhere.

text.tooltip: Prompt naming embeddings by file name; STRING. Installed names get the `embedding:` prefix. Eg: `photo, badhands`

output_tooltips: The prompt with every installed embedding's name prefixed, so 'photo, badhands' becomes 'photo, embedding:badhands'. An embedding that is not installed on this machine is left as written.
Text Parse A1111 Embeddings.name: Text Parse A1111 Embeddings
Text Parse A1111 Embeddings.description: Convert A1111-style embedding names in a prompt to ComfyUI's embedding:name syntax, using the embeddings installed on this machine.

mode.tooltip: Where the replacements come from. `Noodle Soup Prompts` draws from the shared terminology pantry, a published list of subjects, styles and materials that is downloaded once and then cached. `Wildcards` draws one random line from the matching text file in the wildcards directory, where a subfolder is part of the name: __animals/birds__ reads animals/birds.txt.

noodle_key.tooltip: The marker put either side of a term to flag it for replacement. With the default '__', __animals__ is replaced and plain animals is not.

seed.tooltip: Which terms get drawn. Any value other than 0 makes the draw repeatable, so the same seed and the same prompt always give the same words. 0 draws differently every run and cannot be reproduced.

text.tooltip: Prompt with __terms__ to expand; STRING. Each occurrence is drawn separately. Eg: a __animals__ in a __location__

output_tooltips: The prompt with every marked term replaced. A term with no matching pantry entry or wildcard file is left as written.
Text Parse Noodle Soup Prompts.name: Text Parse Noodle Soup Prompts
Text Parse Noodle Soup Prompts.description: Replace __terms__ in a prompt with random Noodle Soup Prompts terminology, or with a random line from the matching wildcard file.

text.tooltip: The prompt to tidy, as `a tabby cat,, a tabby cat`. Typed here, or wired in from whatever built it: Text Concatenate, a style selector, or a caption node.

delimiter.tooltip: What separates one tag from the next in the incoming text. Leave it empty to treat every word as its own tag. Type \n to split a prompt written one tag to a line.

join_with.tooltip: What is put between the tags on the way out. The default ', ' is the ordinary prompt spelling; type \n to get one tag per line, which is easier to read in a saved text file.

dedupe.tooltip: Whether a tag appearing more than once is reduced to one. The survivor keeps the position of the first occurrence, so tidying does not reshuffle the prompt.

ignore_case.tooltip: Whether 'Neon Glow' and 'neon glow' count as the same tag. Off, both survive, which is only useful where a downstream tool treats capitalisation as meaningful.

ignore_emphasis.tooltip: Whether '(neon glow:1.4)' counts as the same tag as 'neon glow'. On with keep set to 'last' is the combination that collapses a prompt onto its weighted spellings, which is normally the intended one, the plain duplicate is usually what a second source contributed.

keep.tooltip: Which of a set of duplicates survives. `first` keeps the earliest spelling, `last` the latest. Position is the first occurrence either way, so keeping the last spelling does not move the tag to the end of the prompt.

remove_empty.tooltip: Whether tags holding nothing are dropped. This is what clears the run of bare commas an unconnected input leaves behind, which otherwise reaches the text encoder as it stands.

collapse_whitespace.tooltip: Whether runs of spaces, tabs and line breaks inside a tag become a single space. This is what removes the line breaks a multi-line prompt box leaves in the middle of a tag.

sort.tooltip: How the surviving tags are ordered. `none` keeps the order they were written in, which is what preserves the weight early tags carry in most encoders. The alphabetical orders make two prompts comparable by eye; `longest first` puts the descriptive phrases ahead of the single words.

limit.tooltip: Keep at most this many tags, counted after everything else has run. 0 keeps all of them. Useful for trimming a caption model's output to the few tags worth keeping.

output_tooltips: The tidied prompt, joined back up with join_with.
The surviving tags as one LIST, for Text List Get and the other list nodes.

The same tags as a STRING list, so a node reading this runs once per tag, one render per tag, for instance. A prompt that tidies down to no tags leaves nothing to run on, so the nodes reading this socket stop and say so; the text output is still delivered, since an empty prompt is a valid one.
How many tags survived.
How many entries the tidy-up took out, counting duplicates, empties and anything past the limit. 0 means the prompt was already clean.
WASPromptTagCleanup.name: WASPromptTagCleanup
WASPromptTagCleanup.description: Split a prompt into tags, drop the duplicates and the empty ones, optionally sort and cap the count, and join it back up. Emphasis such as (tag:1.4) is recognised as the same tag as the plain spelling.

html.tooltip: The document, as HTML. The editor drawn on the node is a view onto this box, so paste markup here and the two stay in step.
html.placeholder: The document, as HTML. The rich text editor writes here.

output_tooltips: The document as HTML, for anything that takes a string. A bare < in the text arrives as <.
WASRichTextEditor.name: WASRichTextEditor
WASRichTextEditor.description: Write a document in a rich text editor drawn on the node and emit it as HTML. The document lives in the node's own text box, so a saved workflow reopens with it intact and a run from the API produces the same text with no browser involved. The box takes no link. Tokens such as [time] and [user] are replaced on the way out, and the box itself is never rewritten. With document.clean_html left on, which is the default, script and iframe elements, object and embed tags, on* handler attributes and javascript: URLs are removed from the output and named in the log; text, styling, images, tables and everything else come through as the box holds them. Setting document.clean_html to false in config.yaml emits the markup untouched.

text.tooltip: Text to search; STRING, as `a tabby cat`. Read only, never changed.
text.placeholder: Eg: a cat on a mat

substring.tooltip: Exact text to look for, taken literally and matched case sensitively, so 'cat' does not find 'Cat'. Filled in, it is what gets searched for and pattern is ignored; leave it empty to search with pattern instead.

pattern.tooltip: Regular expression to search for when substring is empty, for example 'cat|dog' to find either word or '^photo' to require it at the start. An empty pattern matches everything, so leaving both fields blank always reports found.

output_tooltips: True when the substring or the pattern was found anywhere in the text.
Text Find.name: Text Find
Text Find.description: Search text for a plain substring, or for a regular expression when the substring field is left empty.

text.tooltip: Text to search; STRING, as `a tabby cat`. Every filled find box is applied in one pass over it.
text.placeholder: Eg: a cat on a mat

find.placeholder: What to look for. A pattern, so cat|dog matches either
find.tooltip: A regular expression, so 'cat|dog' matches either word and '\s+' matches whitespace. A backslash makes a special character literal. Left empty, nothing is replaced.

replace.placeholder: What each match becomes. Leave empty to delete them
replace.tooltip: What each match becomes. Leave it empty to delete the matches. \1 and \2 stand for the first and second parenthesised group of the pattern, and a literal backslash has to be doubled.

find_2.tooltip: Another pattern, searched in the same single pass as the first. Every pattern is tried against the text as it arrived, so a replacement is never matched again by a later pattern and two patterns can swap. Where two patterns match at the same place, the earlier box wins.

replace_2.tooltip: What the pattern in the box above becomes. Leave it empty to delete what that pattern matched, the same as the first pair.

find_3.tooltip: Another pattern, searched in the same single pass as the first. Every pattern is tried against the text as it arrived, so a replacement is never matched again by a later pattern and two patterns can swap. Where two patterns match at the same place, the earlier box wins.

replace_3.tooltip: What the pattern in the box above becomes. Leave it empty to delete what that pattern matched, the same as the first pair.

find_4.tooltip: Another pattern, searched in the same single pass as the first. Every pattern is tried against the text as it arrived, so a replacement is never matched again by a later pattern and two patterns can swap. Where two patterns match at the same place, the earlier box wins.

replace_4.tooltip: What the pattern in the box above becomes. Leave it empty to delete what that pattern matched, the same as the first pair.

find_5.tooltip: Another pattern, searched in the same single pass as the first. Every pattern is tried against the text as it arrived, so a replacement is never matched again by a later pattern and two patterns can swap. Where two patterns match at the same place, the earlier box wins.

replace_5.tooltip: What the pattern in the box above becomes. Leave it empty to delete what that pattern matched, the same as the first pair.

find_6.tooltip: Another pattern, searched in the same single pass as the first. Every pattern is tried against the text as it arrived, so a replacement is never matched again by a later pattern and two patterns can swap. Where two patterns match at the same place, the earlier box wins.

replace_6.tooltip: What the pattern in the box above becomes. Leave it empty to delete what that pattern matched, the same as the first pair.

find_7.tooltip: Another pattern, searched in the same single pass as the first. Every pattern is tried against the text as it arrived, so a replacement is never matched again by a later pattern and two patterns can swap. Where two patterns match at the same place, the earlier box wins.

replace_7.tooltip: What the pattern in the box above becomes. Leave it empty to delete what that pattern matched, the same as the first pair.

find_8.tooltip: Another pattern, searched in the same single pass as the first. Every pattern is tried against the text as it arrived, so a replacement is never matched again by a later pattern and two patterns can swap. Where two patterns match at the same place, the earlier box wins.

replace_8.tooltip: What the pattern in the box above becomes. Leave it empty to delete what that pattern matched, the same as the first pair.

output_tooltips: The text with every match replaced.
How many replacements were made, for the NUMBER inputs of the suite's own maths and logic nodes. 0 means the text was not matched at all.
The same count as a decimal, for example 3.0.
The same count as a whole number, for a core INT input.
Text Find and Replace.name: Text Find and Replace
Text Find and Replace.description: Replace every regular-expression match in the text and report how many replacements were made.

text.tooltip: Text to fill in; STRING. Blanks written __key__ are swapped for that key's dictionary value; a LIST value is redrawn per blank. Eg: a __animal__ in a __place__

dictionary.tooltip: The replacements; DICT. Each key is a term to look for, its value the replacement. A LIST value has one item drawn per occurrence. Unmatched terms are left as written.

replacement_key.tooltip: Marker put either side of a key; STRING. Eg: __ matches __subject__, not subject.

seed.tooltip: Seed for drawing from LIST values; INT. The same seed rewrites the same text. Ignored for single-value entries. Any whole number; `0` is as good a seed as any.

output_tooltips: The text with every marked term replaced by its entry's value.
Text Find and Replace by Dictionary.name: Text Find and Replace by Dictionary
Text Find and Replace by Dictionary.display_name: Text Find and Replace by Dictionary
Text Find and Replace by Dictionary.description: Replace each delimited term in the text with its value from a dictionary, for example __subject__ with the dictionary's subject entry.
search_aliases: Text Find and Replace by Dictionary

text.tooltip: Text to search; STRING, as `a tabby cat`. Every occurrence of find becomes replace.
text.placeholder: Eg: a cat on a mat

find.tooltip: Exact text to look for, taken literally and matched case sensitively, no pattern characters, unlike Text Find and Replace. An empty search term leaves the text untouched and reports 0 replacements.
find.placeholder: Exact text to look for, taken literally

replace.tooltip: What each occurrence becomes, again taken literally. An empty value deletes the occurrences.
replace.placeholder: What each occurrence becomes. Empty deletes them

output_tooltips: The text with every occurrence of the search term replaced.
How many occurrences were replaced, for the NUMBER inputs of the suite's own maths and logic nodes. 0 means the term was not present.
The same count as a decimal, for example 3.0.
The same count as a whole number, for a core INT input.
Text Find and Replace Input.name: Text Find and Replace Input
Text Find and Replace Input.description: Replace every literal occurrence of the find text and report how many replacements were made. All three text terms come from links.

text_a.tooltip: First text to compare; STRING. Empty boxes count as identical.

text_b.tooltip: Second text to compare; STRING. Both pass through unchanged on TEXT_A_PASS and TEXT_B_PASS.

mode.tooltip: Which measure to report. `similarity` scores how alike the two texts are and lists the words they share; `difference` lists the parts of text_a that changed.

tolerance.tooltip: How loosely a word counts as shared in COMPARISON_TEXT. 0.0 keeps only words appearing in both texts; 1.0 also keeps words one character apart, so 'colour' matches 'color'.

output_tooltips: text_a unchanged, so the node can sit in the middle of a prompt chain instead of on a branch.
text_b unchanged.
True only when the two texts are identical character for character. Neither the mode nor the tolerance affects it.

The score, for the NUMBER inputs of the suite's own maths and logic nodes. In `similarity` mode 1.0 means identical and 0.0 means nothing in common; `difference` mode uses its own scale, which can go past 1.0.

The words behind the comparison, space-separated. In `similarity` mode the words the two texts have in common, and once tolerance is raised the near matches from both. In `difference` mode the parts of text_a that changed.
The same score as a decimal, for a core FLOAT input.
The score with everything after the decimal point dropped, so in `similarity` mode it is 1 only for identical text and 0 for everything else.
Text Compare.name: Text Compare
Text Compare.description: Compare two strings. Both texts pass through unchanged, alongside an exact equality flag, a similarity or difference score, and the words that score was built from. `similarity` scores 1.0 for identical text and falls toward 0.0 as the two diverge, and COMPARISON_TEXT lists the words they have in common. `difference` lists the parts of text_a that changed and scores on a separate scale that is not capped at 1.0, where identical text comes out a little over 1.0. tolerance only widens the words collected in `similarity` mode: it never changes any score, `difference` mode ignores it, and a setting between 0.0 and 1.0 behaves like 0.0.

style1.tooltip: First style to combine, or None to skip it; its prompts come first in both outputs. A style named here and missing from the library empties both outputs rather than dropping part of the prompt silently.

style2.tooltip: Second style, appended after style1. None skips it.

style3.tooltip: Third style, appended after style2. None skips it.

The chosen negative prompts joined with spaces, for a negative CLIP Text Encode. Empty when a named style is missing from the library.
Prompt Multiple Styles Selector.name: Prompt Multiple Styles Selector
Prompt Multiple Styles Selector.description: Concatenate the positive and negative prompts of up to four styles from the style library, separated by spaces. A slot left on None is skipped.

name.tooltip: What to call the style in the selector menu. Eg: cinematic film still. Left empty, the name is made from the date and the first 32 characters of the prompt.

prompt.tooltip: The positive prompt to store; STRING. Eg: `cinematic film still, shallow depth of field, highly detailed`
prompt.placeholder: Eg: cinematic film still, shallow depth of field

negative_prompt.tooltip: The negative prompt to store; STRING. Empty stores a style with no negative half. Eg: `anime, cartoon, low contrast`

output_tooltips: The name the style is stored under, which is the generated one when name was left empty.
The positive prompt as stored, for a positive CLIP Text Encode.
The negative prompt as stored, for a negative CLIP Text Encode.
WASPromptStyleSave.name: WASPromptStyleSave
WASPromptStyleSave.description: Save a positive and negative prompt into the style library under a name, so Prompt Styles Selector can call it back. Saving over a name replaces what it held, and a pair already in the library under another name is left where it is rather than stored twice.

root.tooltip: Which folder the file lands in: ComfyUI's own 'output' or 'temp', or any folder added under paths.allow_write in config.yaml, listed by its own name. filename names the part below it.

filename.tooltip: Name of the file, and any folder below root to put it in. styles.json writes a JSON library, styles.csv writes A1111 columns. Eg: styles/[time(%Y-%m-%d)].json

output_tooltips: The full path of the file that was written.
How many styles were written.
WASPromptStylesExport.name: WASPromptStylesExport
WASPromptStylesExport.description: Write the whole style library out to a file, to share it or back it up. A name ending in .csv writes AUTOMATIC1111's name, prompt and negative_prompt columns; any other name writes JSON. Prompt Styles Import reads either back. A file already at that name is replaced.

file.tooltip: Which style file to read. The menu lists every .json and .csv file in ComfyUI's input, output and temp folders and in any folder added under paths.allow_read in config.yaml, each labelled with the folder it sits in.

mode.tooltip: `add to the library` keeps the styles already saved here and adds the file's. `replace the library` leaves the library holding exactly what the file holds, dropping every other style.

output_tooltips: Every style name in the library after the import, in library order. Text List to Text turns it into one line per name.
How many styles the file held.
How many styles the library holds after the import.
WASPromptStylesImport.name: WASPromptStylesImport
WASPromptStylesImport.description: Read a style library into this one, from a .json library or from an AUTOMATIC1111 styles.csv with name, prompt and negative_prompt columns. The styles land in Prompt Styles Selector's menu. Importing the same file again brings it up to date, dropping the styles it no longer names and keeping every style saved here.

style.tooltip: Which saved style to emit. Each one is a named pair of a positive and a negative prompt. The menu is filled from the style library and shows only 'None' while no style has been saved or imported.

output_tooltips: The style's positive prompt, for a positive CLIP Text Encode. Empty when the style could not be found.
The style's negative prompt, for a negative CLIP Text Encode. Empty when the style has none, or could not be found.
Prompt Styles Selector.name: Prompt Styles Selector
Prompt Styles Selector.description: Emit the positive and negative prompt of a style from the style library. Styles come from styles.json in the config directory, or from the AUTOMATIC1111 styles.csv named by paths.styles, which has to sit in a folder this pack may read.

root.tooltip: Which folder the file lands in: ComfyUI's own 'output' or 'temp', or any folder added under paths.allow_write in config.yaml, listed by its own name. filename names the part below it.

filename.tooltip: Name of the file, and any folder below root to put it in. Eg: nsp_pantry.json, or terminology/[time(%Y-%m-%d)].json to file each day's under a dated name.

scope.tooltip: `the whole pantry` writes every terminology, published words included. `only what you added` writes just the words added from a node or brought in from a file, which is the portable copy of your own additions.

How many words were written, counting every terminology.
WASNoodleSoupPantryExport.name: WASNoodleSoupPantryExport
WASNoodleSoupPantryExport.description: Write the stored Noodle Soup Prompts terminology out as a JSON file, to share it, back it up or edit it by hand. Noodle Soup Pantry Import reads the same file back. A file already at that name is replaced.

file.tooltip: Which pantry file to read. The menu lists every .json file in ComfyUI's input, output and temp folders and in any folder added under paths.allow_read in config.yaml, each labelled with the folder it sits in.

mode.tooltip: `add to the pantry` keeps everything already stored and adds the words the file has that a terminology does not. `replace the pantry` leaves the pantry holding exactly what the file holds, dropping every other terminology.

How many words the file held, counting every terminology.
WASNoodleSoupPantryImport.name: WASNoodleSoupPantryImport
WASNoodleSoupPantryImport.description: Read a Noodle Soup Prompts pantry file into the stored pantry, so a terminology list shared as a file can be used here. The file is a JSON object of terminology name to a list of words, which is what Noodle Soup Pantry Export writes. The file itself is left where it is, and everything read in counts as yours, so a refresh never removes it.

picked.tooltip: One pick per line, as `term: word`. `artist: Greg Rutkowski` takes one word, spelled as the pantry holds it; `artist: *` takes the whole terminology, and so does a line naming one on its own. Blank and `#` lines are ignored, a word named twice goes out once, and line order is output order.

limit.tooltip: How many words go out at most, counting from the first. 0 = every one; 50 = the first 50. `artist` alone holds over 2000.

term.tooltip: One terminology taken whole, added to what is picked above, for wiring the term output of Noodle Soup Term Edit straight in. Eg: `my-animals`. Empty takes only what is picked.

output_tooltips: The picked words, in the order the picked box lists them, a `*` line expanded in pantry order. With nothing picked, the terminology names. Text List to Text joins them with a comma.
The same words, one per line. Feeds the entries box of Noodle Soup Term Edit, and Text Random Line for one word a run.
How many words went out, after limit cut the list.
How many of them were added from a node or brought in from a file rather than supplied by the published pantry.
WASNoodleSoupPick.name: WASNoodleSoupPick
WASNoodleSoupPick.description: Choose words out of the Noodle Soup Prompts pantry and answer them as a list, as text and as a count. The browser panel ticks them; the picked box holds one pick per line either way. With nothing picked the terminology names go out instead, which is how the pantry is read. The yours figure counts what was added from a node or brought in from a file, apart from what the published pantry supplied.

term.tooltip: The terminology name, written without the __ markers. Eg: my-animals, which a prompt then draws from as __my-animals__. A name the pantry does not have yet is created.

action.tooltip: `add entries` stores the words below that the term does not already hold; `remove entries` takes them out and no refresh puts them back; `replace entries` leaves the term holding exactly what is typed; `create the term` makes an empty one; `delete the term` removes it and everything in it.

entries.tooltip: The words to add, remove or store, one per line. Blank lines are skipped. Eg: a line reading 'red fox asleep in long grass'. Ignored by `create the term` and `delete the term`.
entries.placeholder: one word or phrase per line

output_tooltips: The term wrapped in the default markers, __my-animals__, ready to paste into a prompt for Text Parse Noodle Soup Prompts. Empty when the term was deleted.
The terminology name as it was stored, for wiring on to Noodle Soup Pantry Export or another edit. Empty when the term was deleted.
Every entry the term holds after the edit, in draw order. Text List to Text turns it into one line per entry.
How many entries the term holds after the edit.
WASNoodleSoupTermEdit.name: WASNoodleSoupTermEdit
WASNoodleSoupTermEdit.description: Add words to a Noodle Soup Prompts terminology, take words out of one, or make a terminology of your own, so __your_term__ draws from your own list in Text Parse Noodle Soup Prompts and Prompt Parse. Entries you add are kept apart from the ones the bundled pantry supplied, and a later release of that pantry never removes them.

delimiter.tooltip:
Put between the joined pieces; STRING. Eg: ', ' for a prompt, 
 for one per line, empty to run them together.

clean_whitespace.tooltip: Trim whitespace off each piece before joining. `on` also drops a piece holding only spaces.

text_a.tooltip: First piece to join; STRING. Joined with delimiter; empty pieces are skipped. Eg: masterpiece

text_b.placeholder: Second piece, joined after the first

text_c.placeholder: Third piece, joined after the second

output_tooltips: The connected inputs joined in socket order, separated by the delimiter.
Text Concatenate.name: Text Concatenate
Text Concatenate.description: Join up to 24 text inputs with a delimiter, in socket order. Empty inputs are skipped. Type \n as the delimiter to join with newlines.

file.tooltip: Which file to read, one prompt or phrase per line. The menu lists every text file in ComfyUI's input, output and temp folders and in any folder added under paths.allow_read. Ignored when multiline_text is connected.

dictionary_name.tooltip: The key the list of every line is filed under in the dictionary output, so Text Dictionary Get can fetch it again by name. Used exactly as typed.

label.tooltip: Name this batch's read position is remembered under, and the position survives a restart. Two nodes sharing a label share one position and take turns; giving them different labels lets two lists advance independently. Pointing a label at a different file starts it over at the first line.

mode.tooltip: `automatic` hands out the next line on every run and wraps around at the end of the file, which is what walks a list of prompts one per generation. `index` returns the one line asked for and does not advance.

index.tooltip: Which line to return in `index` mode, counting from 0 for the first line. Ignored in `automatic` mode. An index past the end of a file wraps around, so 12 in a 10-line file is line 2.

multiline_text.tooltip: Lines to read instead of file_path; STRING, one entry per line. Anything here overrides file_path.

output_tooltips: The one line selected, stripped of surrounding whitespace. Empty when the file is missing, empty, or the index was out of range.
Every line of the source, as a list filed under dictionary_name, the whole list alongside the single line, for a node that needs all of it.
Text Load Line From File.name: Text Load Line From File
Text Load Line From File.description: Read one line of a text file per prompt, or one line by index. The second output holds every line, keyed by the dictionary name. The file has to sit in a folder this pack may read: ComfyUI's input, output or temp folder, the pack's own folder, or one listed under paths.allow_read in config.yaml. With no path and nothing connected the node logs an error and emits an empty line.

text.tooltip: The text to emit. A line whose first non-blank character is # is left out, so part of a prompt can be parked instead of deleted. Tokens such as [time], [user] and [hostname] are replaced with their values, and a {red|blue} alternation picks one of the options at random unless dynamic_prompts is off.

dynamic_prompts.tooltip: Whether a {red|blue} alternation picks one option at random. `on` is the prompt behaviour; `off` keeps every brace as typed, which is what JSON needs. Lines starting with # are dropped either way, so code belongs in Text Multiline (Code Compatible). The choice is made on the canvas: text sent straight to the API is never rewritten.

output_tooltips: The text with # lines removed and every token replaced.
Text Multiline.name: Text Multiline
Text Multiline.description: A multiline text box. Lines starting with # are dropped, and tokens such as [time] and [user] are substituted. A {red|blue} alternation picks one option at random unless dynamic_prompts is switched off, which keeps a literal brace intact. Text whose # lines have to survive as well, such as code, belongs in Text Multiline (Code Compatible).

text.tooltip: The text to emit, kept exactly as typed. A line starting with `#` survives and a `{red|blue}` alternation is passed through literally, which is what makes this box safe for code and for JSON. Tokens such as [time] and [user] are still replaced.

output_tooltips: The text as typed, with only its tokens replaced.
Text Multiline (Code Compatible).name: Text Multiline (Code Compatible)
Text Multiline (Code Compatible).description: A multiline text box for code, JSON, YAML or anything else that has to arrive exactly as typed. Every line is kept, including one starting with '#', and a {red|blue} alternation is passed through as written. Text Multiline drops # lines and reads braces as a prompt alternation, so this is the box to reach for whenever those two characters mean something.

text.tooltip: Candidates, one per line; STRING, as `a tabby cat`. One line is returned. Blank lines count as candidates.

seed.tooltip: Which line comes out. The same seed and the same text always give the same line; change it to draw a different one. Any whole number; `0` is as good a seed as any.

output_tooltips: The single line the seed selected.
Text Random Line.name: Text Random Line
Text Random Line.description: Pick one line of the incoming text at random, chosen by the seed.

seed.tooltip: Which order comes out. The same seed and the same text always give the same order; change it to shuffle differently. Any whole number; `0` is as good a seed as any.

separator.tooltip: The character the text is cut apart on, and the string the sorted terms are rejoined with. The default ', ' sorts a comma-separated prompt and puts a comma and a space back between each term.

Text Sort.name: Text Sort

Text String Truncate.name: Text String Truncate
Text String Truncate.description: Truncate up to four strings to a number of characters or words, keeping either the beginning or the end.

clip.tooltip: The text encoder that turns the prompt into conditioning. Wire it from the CLIP output of the checkpoint being sampled with, or the prompt will be encoded for the wrong model.

Text to Conditioning.name: Text to Conditioning
Text to Conditioning.description: Encode a linked prompt with a CLIP model, for prompts built by the text nodes rather than typed into a widget.

text.tooltip: Number written as text; STRING. A decimal point gives a decimal, otherwise a whole number. Non-numeric text fails the prompt. Eg: 3.5

output_tooltips: The parsed value, still a whole number or a decimal depending on the text. For the NUMBER inputs of the suite's own maths nodes.
The same value as a decimal, for example 42.0.
The same value as a whole number, with anything after the decimal point dropped: 3.9 becomes 3 and -3.9 becomes -3.
Text to Number.name: Text to Number
Text to Number.description: Parse a string into a number: a float when it contains a decimal point, an int otherwise.

token_name.tooltip: Token name, no brackets; STRING. Expands as [name] in every text node. Empty adds nothing. Eg: season

token_value.tooltip: What the token expands to; STRING. Empty expands to nothing. Eg: late autumn

print_current_tokens.tooltip: `on` logs every custom token now defined and shows them on the node, which is how to check what a previous run left behind; `off` stores the token silently.

Text Add Token by Input.name: Text Add Token by Input
Text Add Token by Input.description: Define a single custom token from a linked name and a linked value, for Text Parse Tokens and every other node that expands [tokens].

tokens.tooltip: One token per line, written as 'name: value', so '[hello]: world' turns [hello] into world in every later node that expands tokens.

print_current_tokens.tooltip: `on` logs every custom token now defined and shows them on the node, which is how to check what a previous run left behind; `off` stores them silently.

Text Add Tokens.name: Text Add Tokens
Text Add Tokens.description: Define custom tokens, one 'name: value' pair per line, for Text Parse Tokens and every other node that expands [tokens]. Only the first colon splits a line, so a value may itself contain colons and drive letters, and a line with no colon, a blank one included, is skipped. The square brackets are convention: the name is matched exactly as written, so a name without them matches bare text anywhere in a prompt.

text.tooltip: Text holding tokens; STRING. [time], [time(%Y-%m-%d)], [hostname], [user], [cuda_device], [cuda_name], plus custom tokens. Eg: render_[time]

output_tooltips: The text with every known token replaced. An unrecognised token is left as written.
Text Parse Tokens.name: Text Parse Tokens
Text Parse Tokens.description: Replace suite tokens such as [time], [hostname] and [user], plus any custom tokens, with their current values.

object.tooltip: The object to animate. It is wrapped rather than changed.

units.tooltip: 'per timeline' spreads the amounts across Three App's loop_seconds, so `180` is 180 degrees per loop and the frame rate only samples it. 'per second' reads them as rates instead, so `90` is a quarter turn a second. 'per capture' spreads them across the frames actually taken, so the same `180` runs end to end whatever the frame count.

rotate_x.tooltip: Degrees per second around X. 0.0 is still, 90.0 is a quarter turn a second.

rotate_y.tooltip: Degrees per second around Y. 30.0 is a slow turntable, negative reverses it.

rotate_z.tooltip: Degrees per second around Z. 0.0 is still, 90.0 is a quarter turn a second.

bob_amplitude.tooltip: How far it rises and falls, in scene units. 0.0 is off, 0.25 is a gentle float.

bob_frequency.tooltip: Bobs per second. 1.0 is one rise and fall a second, 0.25 is languid.

pulse_amplitude.tooltip: How much the scale breathes, as a fraction. 0.0 is off, 0.1 swells it a tenth.

pulse_frequency.tooltip: Pulses per second. 1.0 is one breath a second, 2.0 is twice as quick.

phase.tooltip: Offset into the cycle, in seconds. Give copies 0.0, 0.5 and 1.0 so they do not move in step.

output_tooltips: The moving object, for Three Group or the root socket on Three Scene.
WASThreeAnimateTransform.name: WASThreeAnimateTransform
WASThreeAnimateTransform.description: Move an object continuously. Rotate turns it on each axis, bob slides it up and down, and pulse breathes its scale. With units on 'per second' the amounts are rates. With 'per capture' they are spread across the whole run instead, so 180 degrees over 180 frames needs no arithmetic: set rotate_y to 180 and num_frames to 180. With 'per timeline' they are spread across Three App's loop_seconds, and a render then captures a window out of that longer animation, which is what lets the strip on Three Render pick a part of the motion rather than refit the whole of it. Leaving every amount at 0.0 leaves the object still.

scene.tooltip: What to draw, from Three Scene.

camera.tooltip: Where to draw it from, from either of the Three camera nodes.

antialias.tooltip: `true` smooths the edges of shapes; `false` is faster and leaves visible stair-stepping.

shadows.tooltip: `true` draws shadows, `false` skips them. A light and a mesh must each opt in as well.

orbit_controls.tooltip: `true` lets the viewer be dragged to orbit, wheeled to zoom and middle-dragged to pan; `false` pins the camera.

auto_rotate.tooltip: `true` turns the camera around the target on its own, pausing while it is dragged; `false` holds still.

auto_rotate_speed.tooltip: How fast auto rotate turns. 1.0 is a slow drift, negative turns the other way.

tone_mapping.tooltip: How brightness above 1.0 is brought into range. 'aces' is filmic, 'none' clips, 'agx' is gentler.

exposure.tooltip: Overall brightness into the tone map. 1.0 is neutral, 2.0 one stop up.

loop_seconds.tooltip: How long the whole animation lasts, in seconds. 4.0 is a steady turntable, 20.0 a long move a render takes a few seconds out of. It is the length the viewer loops over, the axis the strip on Three Render is drawn against, and the span every `per timeline` motion is spread across.

pixel_ratio_limit.tooltip: Ceiling on how many device pixels back one CSS pixel. 2.0 is sharp, 1.0 is faster on a large viewer.

shadow_quality.tooltip: Pixels a side of the map every shadow is drawn into. 512 is blocky, 2048 suits most scenes, 8192 costs memory and is for a close crop.

effects.tooltip: The chain of passes the frame is put through, from Three Bloom, Three Depth Of Field or Three Antialias. Left unwired the frame is shown as it was drawn.

output_tooltips: The scene, camera and renderer settings, for Three Viewer.
WASThreeApp.name: WASThreeApp
WASThreeApp.description: Bring a scene and a camera together with the settings the renderer runs under, and hand the result to Three Viewer. Tone mapping decides how brightness above 1.0 is brought into a displayable range: 'aces' is the filmic default, 'none' shows the raw values and clips them. Orbit control lets the viewer be dragged; with it off the camera stays exactly where the camera node put it.

color.tooltip: Colour of the light as hexadecimal. `#ffffff` is white, `#ffd9a0` tungsten.

intensity.tooltip: How brightly the panel gives off light. It is spread over the whole face, so a wider panel at the same number lights no harder. 5.0 is a key light two units across, 40.0 a small bright one.

width.tooltip: How wide the panel is, in scene units. 0.2 throws a hard shadow, 2.0 a soft one, 8.0 an almost shadowless wash.

height.tooltip: How tall the panel is. 2.0 with a 2.0 width is square; 0.1 by 4.0 is a strip light.

shape.tooltip: `rectangle` fills the whole width by height. `disc` rounds it off, for the round highlight a dish or a ring light leaves. Three Render draws both as a rectangle; only a traced render rounds it.

position_x.tooltip: Where the panel sits, across. 0.0 is the middle, 3.0 off to one side.

position_y.tooltip: How high the panel sits. 4.0 is above a subject standing at 0.0.

position_z.tooltip: How far forward the panel sits. 2.0 is between the camera and the subject.

target_x.tooltip: Where the face points, across. 0.0 aims at the middle of the scene.

target_y.tooltip: The height it aims at. 0.0 is the floor, 1.5 the head of a figure.

target_z.tooltip: The depth it aims at. 0.0 aims at the middle of the scene.

output_tooltips: The light, for Three Group or Three Scene.
WASThreeAreaLight.name: WASThreeAreaLight
WASThreeAreaLight.description: Light the scene from a panel with a size rather than from a point, so shadows soften with the width and height given and highlights read as a window or a softbox rather than a pinprick. Three Path Trace Render aims samples straight at it, so it renders cleaner than an emissive material at the same sample count, and the smaller the panel the wider that gap. The panel throws light from one face, the one facing the target. It does not appear in the picture itself, though a mirror reflects it, so pair it with an emissive Three Standard Material where the fitting has to be seen. Three Render lights Three Standard Material and Three Physical Material with it and casts no shadow from it; a traced render shadows and shapes it in full.

color.tooltip: Flat colour as hexadecimal. `#ffffff` is white and leaves a texture's own colours alone.

opacity.tooltip: How solid the surface is, once transparent is on. 1.0 is opaque, 0.35 is a ghost.

transparent.tooltip: `true` honours opacity and an alpha map; `false` draws the surface fully solid.

wireframe.tooltip: `true` draws the triangle edges instead of filled faces; `false` draws solid faces.

side.tooltip: Which faces are drawn. 'front' for closed shapes, 'double' for planes seen from behind.

map.tooltip: The picture to draw. Its colour replaces the colour swatch per pixel.

alpha_map.tooltip: Opacity per pixel, read as greyscale. Needs transparent on to have any effect.

output_tooltips: The surface, for the material socket on Three Mesh.
WASThreeBasicMaterial.name: WASThreeBasicMaterial
WASThreeBasicMaterial.description: A surface that ignores every light and draws its colour flat. Nothing shades it, so a sphere reads as a circle, which is what makes it right for a background card, a UI panel, a wireframe overlay or a texture that must arrive unaltered. It also renders in a scene with no light at all, where a standard material would be black.

width.tooltip: Size along X in scene units. 1.0 is a unit cube, 2.0 twice as wide.

height.tooltip: Size along Y in scene units. 1.0 is a unit cube, 0.1 a flat slab.

depth.tooltip: Size along Z in scene units. 1.0 is a unit cube, 0.1 a thin panel.

width_segments.tooltip: How many divisions across X. 1 leaves flat faces, 32 gives a shader room to bend them.

height_segments.tooltip: How many divisions across Y. 1 leaves flat faces, 32 gives a shader room to bend them.

depth_segments.tooltip: How many divisions across Z. 1 leaves flat faces, 32 gives a shader room to bend them.

output_tooltips: The box shape, for the geometry socket on Three Mesh.
WASThreeBoxGeometry.name: WASThreeBoxGeometry
WASThreeBoxGeometry.description: A rectangular box, sized in scene units and centred on its own origin. Wire it into Three Mesh together with a material. Segment counts subdivide each face, which matters only where a shader or a displacement map needs vertices to move; one segment a side is right for a plain box. The shape is described here and built in the browser, so nothing is rendered on the server.

app.tooltip: The scene, camera and renderer settings, from Three App.

filename_prefix.tooltip: Leading part of the file name, as `three_scene`. A `/` in it makes sub-folders under the chosen root.

root.tooltip: Which of ComfyUI's folders the archive is written into, as `output` or `temp`.

title.tooltip: Title the page carries, shown in the browser tab. `Three.js scene` by default.

output_tooltips: Where the archive was written, as a path.
How many files went into the archive, textures included.
WASThreeCompile.name: WASThreeCompile
WASThreeCompile.description: Write the scene out as a zip holding a web page that runs on its own. Unpack it and open index.html: the scene draws, and the camera can be orbited, with no ComfyUI and nothing fetched over the network. Three.js, the scene description and every texture go in the archive, and each texture address is rewritten to point at its copy. A scene using Three Custom Geometry, Custom Material, Custom Object, Custom Update or Script Module carries that JavaScript into the page, so the archive is code as well as data, and is refused unless threejs.allow_scripts is on in config.yaml.

javascript.tooltip: A body returning a geometry, as `return new THREE.LatheGeometry(points);`. `THREE` is in scope.

output_tooltips: The shape the code returned, for the geometry socket on Three Mesh.
WASThreeCustomGeometry.name: WASThreeCustomGeometry
WASThreeCustomGeometry.description: Reach any Three.js geometry class the pack has no node for, by returning one from a short JavaScript body. `THREE` is in scope, so a torus knot, a lathe, a tube or a hand-built BufferGeometry are all one line away. The code runs in your browser when the viewer loads, with the same reach as any frontend extension, so only run a workflow carrying custom JavaScript if you trust where it came from.

module.tooltip: Which module builds the material. The menu lists every `.js` and `.txt` file opening with `// was-threejs-module 1` in ComfyUI's input, output and temp folders and in any folder under paths.allow_read.

texture1.tooltip: A texture the module receives under the name its header declares. The first declared texture arrives here, the second in the slot below, and so on.

texture2.tooltip: A texture the module receives under the name its header declares. The first declared texture arrives here, the second in the slot below, and so on.

texture3.tooltip: A texture the module receives under the name its header declares. The first declared texture arrives here, the second in the slot below, and so on.

texture4.tooltip: A texture the module receives under the name its header declares. The first declared texture arrives here, the second in the slot below, and so on.

output_tooltips: The surface the module returned, for the material socket on Three Mesh.
WASThreeCustomMaterial.name: WASThreeCustomMaterial
WASThreeCustomMaterial.description: Reach any Three.js material class the pack has no node for, from a module file you place in ComfyUI's input folder or a folder under paths.allow_read. The module's header names the textures it wants and the node's slots take those names. Code is never typed on the node and never travels inside a workflow, so a graph from someone else cannot bring javascript with it. A module runs in your browser when the viewer loads, with the same reach as any frontend extension, and only while threejs.allow_scripts is on.

javascript.tooltip: A body returning an Object3D, as `return new THREE.InstancedMesh(geometry1, material1, 100);`.

geometry1.tooltip: A shape reachable in the body as `geometry1`.

geometry2.tooltip: A shape reachable in the body as `geometry2`.

material1.tooltip: A surface reachable in the body as `material1`.

material2.tooltip: A surface reachable in the body as `material2`.

object1.tooltip: An object reachable in the body as `object1`, to add or to place.

object2.tooltip: An object reachable in the body as `object2`, to add or to place.

output_tooltips: The object the code returned, for Three Group or Three Scene.
WASThreeCustomObject.name: WASThreeCustomObject
WASThreeCustomObject.description: Build any Object3D from a short JavaScript body, for what wiring cannot express: scattering a hundred copies, an InstancedMesh, a Points cloud, LineSegments. `THREE` is in scope and whatever is wired in arrives as `geometry1`, `geometry2`, `material1`, `material2`, `object1` and `object2`. The code runs in your browser when the viewer loads, with the same reach as any frontend extension, so only run a workflow carrying custom JavaScript if you trust where it came from.

object.tooltip: The object the code moves. It is wrapped rather than changed.

javascript.tooltip: A body run each frame, as `object.position.y = Math.sin(time) * 0.5;`. Nothing is returned.

output_tooltips: The moving object, for Three Group or the root socket on Three Scene.
WASThreeCustomUpdate.name: WASThreeCustomUpdate
WASThreeCustomUpdate.description: Run a short JavaScript body on an object once per drawn frame, for motion Three Animate Transform cannot express. In scope are `object`, `time` in seconds since the viewer started, `delta` in seconds since the last frame, `THREE`, and `ctx` for anything to be kept between frames. Scaling by `delta` keeps the motion the same speed whatever the frame rate. The code runs in your browser, so only run a workflow carrying custom JavaScript if you trust where it came from.

radius_top.tooltip: Radius at the top. 0.0 closes it to a point, which makes a cone.

radius_bottom.tooltip: Radius at the base. Matching radius_top at 1.0 gives a straight cylinder.

height.tooltip: Height along Y in scene units. 1.0 is as tall as a unit cube.

radial_segments.tooltip: Divisions around the axis. 32 looks round, 6 gives a hexagonal prism.

height_segments.tooltip: Divisions along the height. 1 is enough unless a shader has to bend it.

open_ended.tooltip: `true` leaves the flat caps off, making a pipe; `false` closes both ends.

output_tooltips: The cylinder shape, for the geometry socket on Three Mesh.
WASThreeCylinderGeometry.name: WASThreeCylinderGeometry
WASThreeCylinderGeometry.description: A cylinder standing on Y, and a cone or a truncated cone when the two radii differ. Setting the top radius to 0.0 gives a point, so a cone is this node with one number changed. Open ended leaves the flat caps off, which is what makes a pipe rather than a solid.

strength.tooltip: How much glow is added. 0.3 is a hint, 0.6 usual, 2.0 heavy.

radius.tooltip: How far the glow spreads. 0.1 is tight around a highlight, 1.0 a wide haze.

threshold.tooltip: How bright a pixel has to be before it glows. 0.85 catches highlights alone, 0.0 makes the whole frame glow.

input.tooltip: The effect before this one, if any. Left unwired this is the first pass after the scene is drawn.

output_tooltips: The chain so far, for the next effect or for Three App's effects socket.
WASThreeBloom.name: WASThreeBloom
